## 1 Introduction {#s-1}

### 1.1 Foreword {#s-1-1}

European Digital Identity Wallets form part of a cross-border trust infrastructure in which software defects, compromised dependencies and unremediated vulnerabilities can affect not only an individual wallet unit, but also Wallet Providers, PID Providers, relying parties and confidence in the national electronic identification scheme.

Secure software development, secure maintenance and effective vulnerability management are therefore continuing assurance conditions throughout the lifecycle of the wallet solution and the services on which it depends.

This document translates that lifecycle perspective into requirements and guidance for Wallet Providers and PID Providers operating under the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System. It complements the certification and governance framework established by NL-SYS-01 by defining practices for product cybersecurity risk management, secure development and maintenance, third-party component governance, verification and validation, monitoring, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, remediation, security updates and secure decommissioning.

The document is informed by Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act), the applicable EUDI Wallet implementing acts and relevant standards. References to the Cyber Resilience Act express alignment with its lifecycle and vulnerability-handling principles. They do not, by themselves, determine whether a specific wallet component, provider or service falls within the legal scope of that Regulation.

The requirements are intended to support consistent implementation and assessable evidence while avoiding duplication with applicable product, organisational or service certification. They shall be read together with NL-SYS-01 and the applicable Wallet Provider and PID Provider certification schemes.

### 1.2 Scope {#s-1-2}

This document specifies lifecycle requirements and supporting guidance for secure software development, secure maintenance and vulnerability management by Wallet Providers and PID Providers within the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System.

It applies to the software and related processes used to develop, build, test, release, operate, maintain and decommission EUDI Wallet mobile applications and the Remote Data Processing Solutions (RDPS), interfaces, build and distribution services, and third-party components on which those applications depend.

The requirements cover product cybersecurity risk management; cybersecurity planning and requirements; architecture and design; secure implementation; technical documentation and software bills of materials; verification and validation; secure production and distribution; monitoring and issue management; third-party component management; coordinated vulnerability disclosure; remediation; security updates; and secure decommissioning. They apply throughout the support period and shall be revisited when the product, its dependencies, its operational environment, the threat landscape or applicable legal and technical requirements change.

For the purposes of this document, secure maintenance includes the controlled modification of software and dependencies, continued verification of security controls, monitoring for newly disclosed vulnerabilities, risk-based remediation, release of security updates and communication of residual risks. Vulnerability management includes intake, triage, risk evaluation, coordination, disclosure, remediation, testing, release and post-release monitoring.

This document does not replace the functional, organisational or product-security requirements contained in the applicable EUDI Wallet legislation, implementing acts, EU cybersecurity certification schemes or NL certification schemes. Nor does it establish whether Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 or national NIS2 legislation applies to a particular provider or product. Where such legislation applies, its mandatory provisions prevail.

This document also does not prescribe all security properties of the wallet solution itself; those properties remain governed by the applicable certification requirements, architecture, risk assessment and technical specifications.

## 2 Legal Basis & References {#s-2}

### 2.1 Legal Basis {#s-2-1}

The legal basis for these requirements is formed by the Union and applicable national legislation governing European Digital Identity Wallets, electronic identification, cybersecurity risk management and incident reporting.

The following instruments are particularly relevant:

- Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, establishing the European Digital Identity Framework.
- Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, known as the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), including essential cybersecurity and vulnerability-handling requirements throughout the product lifecycle.
- Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, where the provider or certified service falls within its scope or where its technical and methodological requirements are adopted by the applicable national framework.
- Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1502 concerning assurance levels for electronic identification means, including assurance level High.

Where national transposition or sector-specific rules impose more specific or stricter requirements, those requirements prevail. The applicant shall identify the competent authority, applicable reporting obligations and any sector-specific cybersecurity requirements relevant to its certified services.

## 3 Relationships with NIS2, CRA {#s-3}

### 3.1 Relationship with NIS2 {#s-3-1}

Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, establishes the legal and trust framework for European Digital Identity Wallets and requires wallet solutions to satisfy applicable functional, security and certification requirements. Within the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System, NL-SYS-01 organises how the wallet and the electronic identification scheme under which it is provided are brought together through interrelated conformity assessments and continuing certification controls.

Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2) addresses cybersecurity at entity and service level. Where a Wallet Provider, PID Provider or a supporting service falls within its scope as transposed into national law, the entity is required to implement proportionate cybersecurity riskmanagement measures and comply with the applicable incident-reporting obligations. Article 21 of NIS2 expressly includes supply-chain security, security in network and information systems acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling and disclosure, policies and procedures to assess the effectiveness of cybersecurity riskmanagement measures, and the use of cryptography and encryption.

The eIDAS and NIS2 frameworks are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable. eIDAS and its implementing acts establish wallet-specific trust, functionality, security and certification outcomes. NIS2 establishes entity-level governance, risk management, supplychain, business-continuity and incident-reporting duties where applicable. Secure software development, secure maintenance and vulnerability management provide the operational link between those layers by ensuring that certified wallet-related services continue to manage software and dependency risks after initial development and certification.

The requirements in this document support that link by requiring traceable cybersecurity planning, secure design and implementation, controlled development environments, component inventories and SBOMs, recurring verification and validation, monitoring of vulnerabilities and incidents, coordinated disclosure, risk-based remediation, security updates and post-release review. Evidence generated through these activities may support both continued certification under the NL system and demonstration of relevant NIS2 controls, but conformity with this document does not by itself establish full compliance with NIS2 or national implementing legislation.

### 3.2 Relationship with CRA {#s-3-2}

Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), establishes horizontal cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements. Its subject matter includes essential cybersecurity requirements for the design, development and production of such products and essential requirements for the vulnerability-handling processes maintained during the period in which the product is expected to be in use. The CRA therefore expresses a lifecycle model in which security is designed into the product, maintained after release and supported by effective vulnerability handling and security updates.

An EUDI Wallet solution comprises software with security-critical functions and may depend on mobile applications, wallet secure cryptographic applications or devices, backend RDPS, interfaces, build and signing infrastructure, software libraries and distribution platforms. A weakness in any of these elements can affect wallet integrity, confidentiality, availability, authenticity, sole control by the user, protection of person identification data or trust in the electronic identification scheme. For that reason, CRA-aligned secure-development and vulnerability-handling practices are directly relevant to the EUDI Wallet assurance context, even where the legal applicability or classification of a particular component under the CRA must be determined separately.

This document adopts the CRA's lifecycle logic as a state-of-the-art baseline for the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System. It requires product-context and risk documentation; security requirements and architecture; secure implementation and development environments; component and dependency inventories, including SBOMs; verification and validation; protection of build, signing and distribution processes; monitoring throughout the support period; coordinated vulnerability disclosure; risk-based remediation; testing and release of security updates; and secure decommissioning.

In the EUDI Wallet context, these practices also support continued conformity after initial certification. Changes to wallet software, RDPS, third-party components, cryptographic mechanisms, supported mobile platforms or the threat landscape can invalidate assumptions on which certification evidence was based. The resulting change, vulnerability and remediation records shall therefore feed the applicable surveillance, change-notification, incident-management and certificate-maintenance processes defined by NL-SYS-01 and the relevant Wallet Provider, PID Provider and product certification schemes.

Alignment with the CRA is not intended to create a parallel certification route or to treat CRA conformity as a substitute for EUDI Wallet certification. The applicable eIDAS requirements, implementing acts, EU cybersecurity certification requirements and NL scheme rules remain authoritative for the certification target. Conversely, certification under the NL EUDI Wallet Certification System does not automatically demonstrate CRA conformity where the CRA applies; the responsible economic operator must separately establish the applicable CRA obligations, conformity-assessment route, technical documentation, reporting duties and market-surveillance requirements.

The technical content of this document draws on the standardisation work supporting the CRA, in particular the draft CEN/CENELEC JTC 13/WG 9 work on product cybersecurity risk management, the product lifecycle and vulnerability handling. It also considers the draft CEN/CENELEC TC 224/WG 17 work relevant to identity-management and access-control products.

Mandatory requirements and non-mandatory guidance are distinguished throughout this document. Requirements apply to the relevant provider or manufacturer within the scope assigned by the applicable certification scheme. Guidance explains recognised implementation approaches but does not create an additional obligation unless incorporated by a normative requirement or by another applicable legal or scheme provision.

## 4 Product Cybersecurity Risk Management {#s-4}

### 4.1 Introduction {#s-4-1}

Risk management is a continuous activity that spans the entire product lifecycle -from design and development through production, maintenance, and decommissioning - ensuring cybersecurity remains appropriate for the product's intended purpose and foreseeable use. Changes in circumstances, such as significant design modifications or shifts in the threat landscape, may necessitate revisiting risk management activities, particularly risk assessments, to keep residual risk within accepted bounds.

The risk management process consists of six interconnected activities: establishing the product context, defining risk acceptance criteria, risk assessment (encompassing asset identification, risk analysis, risk evaluation and acceptance), treating identified risks, communicating residual risks, and ongoing monitoring and review. These activities will be laid out in the following sub clauses.

See OpenCRE 307-242 at opencre.org/cre/307-242 for related resources and topics for guidance.

### 4.2 Product Context Documentation {#s-4-2}

## Introduction

Establishing the product context is the foundational step for identifying and treating cybersecurity risks associated with a product. It is an iterative activity that needs to be revisited whenever the product or its environment changes throughout the product lifecycle.

The product context encompasses several interrelated elements: the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use, the product's functions, its operational environment, an architectural overview of its components and interfaces, any Remote Data Processing Solutions (RDPS), a description of its users, and an overview of how cybersecurity functions are distributed across the product and its environment. Together, these elements define the scope within which risks are identified, assessed, and treated.

Output: documentation containing the product context.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.2-CR-01

The product context shall be identified and documented, covering the product's intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use (IPRFU), its functions, its operational environment, an architectural overview, a description of its users including their experience level and security-relevant objectives, and where relevant and useful: general product insights from the market segments involved, including market expectations.

Source: RMA-01-RQ-01, Input clause (40000-1-2 6.2)

## Guidance

- IPRFU: Document the conditions of use for which the product is designed, including scenarios that are not intended but can reasonably be foreseen. Consider accessibility, including the use of Assistive Technology, as part of this scope.

- Product functions: Include both functional features and cybersecurity-specific features (e.g., functions that protect the product or safeguard user health and safety), as well as any configuration capabilities.
- Operational environment: Describe the networks, systems, and physical setting in which the product will be used or could reasonably be expected to be used. Characterize the applicable physical and logical access levels (for example public, restricted, or controlled). External systems and people capable of influencing the product's functions should also be treated as part of this operational environment.
- Architecture overview: Provide a high-level overview of the product's key components, interfaces, and dependencies. Highlight how integrated components introduce cybersecurity risks and what cybersecurity features they provide or require. Where RDPS is present, describe its role in delivering product functions.
- User description: Classify users according to their expected level of experience and capability - for example, as vulnerable, ordinary, instructed, or skilled users - and identify their security-relevant objectives (e.g., data confidentiality, protection against fraud, health and safety). Note that a single product may serve multiple user groups in different contexts.
- Distribution of cybersecurity functions: Record which security functions the product supplies for its own use, which ones it instead relies on the environment to provide, and which ones it offers for other products to use. This is not a one-time exercise - since adding a control to the product can itself alter the product context, it may need to be revisited.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.2-CR-02

Where the product includes remote data processing solutions (RDPS), the RDPS shall be considered to be included in the product context.

Source: RMA-01-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

- The operational environment description should include connectivity characteristics, expected availability, data handled, and expected uptime constraints relevant to the RDPS.
- Where relevant, RDPS should be reflected consistently across all product context elements, including IPRFU, functions, architecture, and user description.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.2-CR-03

A documented procedure shall be maintained for establishing and updating the product context, including defined triggers for re-evaluation when the application, its RDPS, or its operational environment changes.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Triggers for re-evaluation may include: release of a new application version, changes to backend RDPS infrastructure, changes to third-party SDK or library dependencies, changes to target platform (iOS/Android OS version), changes to data processing scope, or changes to the intended user population. The procedure should define roles responsible for initiating and approving product context updates and should reference the output artefacts (e.g., product context document, architecture overview) that need to be revised.

### 4.3 Risk Acceptance Criteria {#s-4-3}

## Introduction

Risk acceptance criteria establish the threshold at which identified risks are considered tolerable, either without further treatment or after mitigation measures have been applied. These criteria reflect the product context and are typically defined at the beginning of the risk assessment process, although they may need to be reviewed and updated as the threat landscape, state of the art, or product lifecycle changes.

Output: Documented risk acceptance criteria for the product’s cybersecurity.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.3-CR-01

The cybersecurity risk acceptance criteria shall be established. At minimum, the criteria shall account for the product context, regulatory factors, supply chain aspects, the nature of risks, the current state of the art, and user needs.

Source: RMA-02-RQ-01 (40000-1-2) and corresponding assessment criteria (user needs)

## Guidance

Several factors commonly inform these criteria:

- the product's intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use;
- applicable regulatory requirements;
- supply chain considerations including contractual agreements, downstream integrators, and reasonable user expectations;
- operational environment characteristics;
- the scale of deployment - a risk acceptable for a single product instance may become unacceptable when aggregated across a large installed base;
- how severe the impact would be and how likely the risk and any consequences it brings are to occur;
- nature of the risks, such as the health and safety of individuals affected;
- user needs;
- and the user population's capacity to further mitigate residual risk.

In some circumstances, deviation from established criteria may be justified - for instance, when a user explicitly accepts certain risks through contractual agreement. Where residual risk is transferred, clear communication to relevant parties is essential.

Risk acceptance criteria are not static - they should be reviewed and updated when relevant circumstances change, such as shifts in the threat landscape, changes in applicable legislation, or transitions in the product or component lifecycle (e.g., obsolescence or deprecation). When defining criteria, consider that some risks may be inherently necessary for the product to function; such risks may be acceptable under the criteria provided the product context and relevant communication are accounted for.

Aggregated risk from large mobile install bases can transform individually low-severity risks into systemic threats, particularly for vulnerabilities exploitable at scale (e.g., credential harvesting, silent data exfiltration, botnet enrollment). The process should define explicit thresholds or scaling factors at which individual-instance risk acceptance decisions are reexamined. This is particularly relevant for widely distributed consumer mobile applications.

The OWASP Mobile Top 10 typically provides example attack scenarios that illustrate the potential impact of prevalent mobile application security weaknesses, including, in some cases, impact across large user populations

NOTE: Some product categories are covered by a vertical (sector-specific) standard that already defines its own risk acceptance criteria and metrics; where such a standard exists, applying its criteria is considered justified and consistent with the state of the art for that category.

Mobile-specific factors that may inform risk acceptance thresholds include: the heterogeneity of end-user devices and OS versions in the installed base; the inability to enforce timely patch adoption across user populations; the exposure of the application to shared-device or rooted/jailbroken environments; and the dependency on platform-enforced security controls (e.g., iOS App Transport Security, Android Keystore). OWASP MASVS provides a structured baseline of security controls for mobile applications that can serve as a reference point when calibrating what constitutes an acceptable residual risk level for a given mobile product category.

### 4.4 Product Cybersecurity Asset Identification {#s-4-4}

## Introduction

Product cybersecurity asset identification establishes what needs to be protected for the product. Assets are closely tied to the product's context and span a broad range: data stored, processed, or transmitted (such as cryptographic keys, personal data, and logs); functions the product performs; software and hardware components and their interfaces; update and patch processes; and the wider system environment including adjacent networks and devices. Beyond the product itself, assets may relate to the user's high-level objectivessuch as health, safety, privacy, user data, and availability of functions-as well as to the broader environment, including other persons, domestic animals, and public interest.

Output: an inventory of the product's cybersecurity assets together with the cybersecurity properties associated with each.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.4-CR-01

When conducting a product cybersecurity risk assessment, all cybersecurity assets relevant to the product shall be identified, and it shall be determined which cybersecurity properties (confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and others as applicable) need to be ensured for each. This identification shall be grounded in the product context established under section 5.2, and the resulting asset list with associated cybersecurity properties shall be included in the product's technical documentation. The asset scope is broad and shall consider data assets (e.g. credentials, keys, personal data, configuration data, safety signals, firmware images, logs), functional assets, hardware and software components and interfaces, user-objective assets (health, safety, privacy, availability), and environmental assets (adjacent networks, third parties, public interest, and assets involved in RDPS).

## Source:

- RMA-03-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)
- REQ-KEV-001 (40000-10)

- Related output obligation (40000-1-2 6.4.2.4)
- SOTA: Gap analysis findings on: documentation obligation, authenticity as a named property, safety signals as a discrete asset type

## Guidance

Asset identification should be conducted in a manner that is representative of the product within its specified product context. The following guidance supports practitioners in scoping the exercise:

- Assets may be grouped into categories: product-level data assets, functional assets, supporting/operational assets (components, interfaces, update processes), userobjective assets, and environmental assets.
- Examples of data assets worth considering include credentials, cryptographic keys and authentication tokens, personal and financial data, safety signals, configuration data, firmware images, logs, and access rights.
- For each identified asset, the cybersecurity properties to be ensured should be explicitly indicated. Relevant properties include confidentiality, integrity, availability, and authenticity. Other properties may be applicable depending on the product context.

NOTE 1: Enumerating critical assets focuses security controls and testing on what needs to be protected, supporting a risk-proportionate approach to cybersecurity.

NOTE 2: Mobile applications frequently act as entry points to backend systems. Impact assessment should therefore consider: the sensitivity and volume of data accessible via the RDPS if the mobile application is compromised; the potential for lateral movement from a compromised mobile client to backend infrastructure; and the number of users whose data or services could be affected through a single exploited vulnerability in the mobile application.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.4-CR-02

In case the application employs AI models, AI-specific assets shall be included in the considerations to identify cybersecurity assets.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Potentially relevant AI-specific assets include training data, test data, input data, model storage, augmentation data, agentic working memory, system prompts.

Further guidance is provided in ISO/IEC 27090, prEN 18282, and the OWASP AI Exchange which is designed to present the consensus of these standards.

### 4.5 Product Cybersecurity Risk Identification {#s-4-5}

## Introduction

Product cybersecurity risk identification builds on the previously identified assets to determine which threats could realistically affect those assets within the product's context. Not every threat automatically constitutes a risk; the process evaluates whether a threat could cause an incident that compromises an asset and thereby gives rise to a cybersecurity risk.

Threat modelling provides a structured method for this identification, taking into account factors such as the product lifecycle, its functional behaviour, and the capabilities and motives of potential threat actors. Publicly available threat catalogues and sector-specific resources can support this process. Beyond threats, vulnerabilities - weaknesses in the product that threat actors could exploit - represent a distinct category of risk. Awareness of known vulnerabilities, discoverable through publicly available databases, is essential to addressing them appropriately. The applicability of identified threats and vulnerabilities is assessed by estimating exploitability within the defined product context, after which applicable items are documented as product cybersecurity risks.

Output: a list containing the product cybersecurity risks.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.5-CR-01

Drawing on the established product context, product cybersecurity risks shall be identified. Each identified risk shall specify which asset(s) are targeted, which cybersecurity objective(s) of those assets may be compromised, and the cause of that potential compromise.

Source: RMA-04-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Threat modelling is a recommended method for systematically identifying cybersecurity risks in mobile applications. Common approaches include STRIDE, attack trees, and PASTA; sector-specific risk analysis methods may also be used where applicable.

Useful inputs include mobile threat catalogues and knowledge bases such as MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS), and the OWASP Mobile Top 10, as well as platform-specific guidance from Android and iOS.

Not every identified threat constitutes a cybersecurity risk. The assessment should determine whether, in the specific mobile application context, the threat could realistically lead to an incident affecting assets such as user data, credentials, cryptographic keys, backend access, or app integrity.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.5-CR-02

Where publicly known vulnerabilities exist that are relevant to the product's assets and their associated cybersecurity properties, those publicly known vulnerabilities shall be identified. This obligation is conditional on the availability of such information.

Source: RMA-04-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Known vulnerabilities can be identified through publicly available vulnerability databases. Awareness of these vulnerabilities is a prerequisite for addressing the associated risks. Even where exploitation may not be immediately apparent, the presence of a known vulnerability in the product warrants documentation as a potential product cybersecurity risk.

Vulnerabilities represent a specific category of risk arising from weaknesses in the product that threat actors could exploit. The applicability of a known vulnerability to the product should be assessed in the context of the product's exploitability within the defined product context.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.5-CR-03

A documented threat modelling procedure specific to mobile applications shall be established and maintained, defining the methodology to be applied (e.g., STRIDE, PASTA, attack trees), the threat catalogues to use, the roles responsible for conducting threat modelling, and the trigger conditions under which threat modelling shall be performed or repeated (e.g., new feature introduction, platform OS update, third-party SDK integration).

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

The procedure should specify how mobile-specific threat surfaces are addressed, including: client-side attack vectors (e.g., reverse engineering, tampering, repackaging), inter-process communication mechanisms, and interactions with Remote Data Processing Solutions.

Threat catalogues should incorporate mobile-relevant threat taxonomies, including MITRE ATT&CK for Mobile (https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/mobile/), which covers tactics and techniques specific to Android and iOS platforms, and OWASP Mobile Top 10. Entries should be mapped to the asset categories and annotated with relevance to RDPS interactions (e.g., insecure API endpoints, token interception). The review interval should be risk-proportionate but no less frequent than annually, or following a significant change to the mobile platform ecosystem (e.g., a major Android or iOS release introducing new attack surfaces).

In case the application employs AI models, relevant threat taxonomies can be found in ISO/IEC 27090, prEN 18282, and the OWASP AI Exchange, which is designed to present the consensus of these standards.

### 4.6 Product Cybersecurity Risk Analysis {#s-4-6}

## Introduction

This document does not require one specific risk analysis method. Different methods may be used, provided that the risk estimate considers both the likelihood of a successful attack and the impact if that attack succeeds. Possible approaches include fishbone diagrams, event tree analysis, fault tree analysis, attack feasibility ratings, or attack potential assessments.

Product cybersecurity risk analysis aims to estimate both the likelihood of occurrence and the potential impact of cybersecurity incidents arising from identified product risks. These estimates may be expressed qualitatively (e.g., using risk matrices) or quantitatively (e.g., using numerical scoring systems), and should be applied consistently to enable informed decisions on risk treatment or acceptance. Both likelihood and impact are assessed from the perspective of the users potentially affected. Likelihood factors may include how easily a risk can be discovered and how quickly it can materialize, while impact factors may include exposure of sensitive data, account takeover, fraud enablement, data loss, economic harm, and loss of accessibility.

Output: documented likelihood, impact severity, and incident scenario for each identified risk, including a rationale.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.6-CR-01

For each product cybersecurity risk identified in accordance with 5.5, the likelihood of the associated cybersecurity incident occurring shall be estimated.

Source: RMA-05-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

When estimating likelihood, consider factors such as the discoverability of the risk and the speed at which it could materialize. Some risks may be easily detected by users, while others may be exploited without the user's awareness or so rapidly that intervention is not possible.

Likelihood estimates should be informed by current threat intelligence rather than solely by theoretical analysis. Relevant sources include: Apple Platform Security documentation and iOS Security Advisories, Android Security Bulletins published by Google, CVE databases filtered for mobile platform components, and OWASP Mobile Top 10 for prevalent mobile attack categories. The organization should establish a process for reviewing these sources at defined intervals (e.g., quarterly) and reassessing likelihood estimates when significant new threat information is published.

When estimating likelihood, the analysis should consider how exploitability is for relevant threat actors, taking into account their capabilities, access, and motivation. Threat actors may include external attackers, malicious apps on the same device, insiders, or unauthorized users with physical or logical access to the device or application.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.6-CR-02

For each product cybersecurity risk identified in accordance with 5.5, the severity of impact of the associated cybersecurity incident shall be estimated.

Source: RMA-05-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

When estimating impact, consider dimensions such as health and safety consequences, data loss, economic losses to the user, and effects on accessibility. As with likelihood, impact may be expressed qualitatively or quantitatively and should reflect the perspective of the users potentially affected by the risk.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.6-CR-03

For each product cybersecurity risk identified in accordance with 5.5, the cybersecurity incident scenario in which that risk could materialize shall be documented.

Source: RMA-05-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Risk scenarios describe the context in which a risk could materialize into a cybersecurity incident. Documenting scenarios supports consistent analysis and enables informed risk treatment decisions.

The organization should structure risk scenarios using a defined template that captures the threat actor or source, the attack vector applicable to the mobile application or its RDPS, the vulnerability or weakness exploited, the attack path, and the resulting harm to the user.

For mobile applications, the attack vector field should reflect mobile-specific vectors such as: malicious applications on the same device, network-based attacks exploiting insecure communication, physical access to an unlocked or unencrypted device, and supply chain compromise of third-party SDKs or libraries integrated into the application. OWASP MASTG threat modelling guidance and OWASP Mobile Top 10 (2016/2024) provide reference scenario structures applicable to mobile contexts. STRIDE or PASTA methodologies can be adapted for mobile scenario structuring. EN 18037 also provides guidance on risk scenario structuring.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.6-CR-04

A repeatable risk analysis methodology for cybersecurity risks shall be defined and documented, specifying the rating scale, criteria, and scoring rationale to be applied consistently across all risk assessments.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

The methodology should define discrete likelihood levels (e.g., rare, unlikely, possible, likely, almost certain) with explicit criteria for each level. For mobile-specific contexts, criteria may reference factors such as: public availability of exploit code targeting the mobile platform (iOS/Android), ease of exploitation given typical mobile threat actor capabilities, and whether the attack requires physical device access, network proximity, or can be conducted remotely. The methodology should be documented in a risk assessment procedure and applied uniformly by all analysts performing assessments. OWASP MASTG and OWASP Mobile Top 10(2016/2024) provide reference threat scenarios that can inform likelihood criteria calibration.

The impact methodology should extend general impact categories (health and safety, data loss, economic harm, accessibility) with mobile-specific sub-categories, such as: exposure of data processed or stored by the mobile application (including data accessible via platform APIs such as contacts, location, camera, and biometric data); loss of control over device functions that could affect the user or third parties; and cascading impact on backend Remote Data Processing Solutions (RDPS) accessed by the application. OWASP MASVS v2 (particularly the MASVS-STORAGE, MASVS-PRIVACY, and MASVS-RESILIENCE categories) provides a structured taxonomy of mobile-specific impact areas that can inform impact criteria definition. NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Table H-2 provides a general impact taxonomy that can be adapted for mobile contexts.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.6-CR-05

The rationale and evidence supporting each likelihood and severity result shall be documented, enabling independent review and auditability of the risk analysis.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

For each risk, the risk record should capture: the likelihood rating assigned, the criteria applied from the defined methodology, the evidence or assumptions supporting the rating (e.g., known exploitation in the wild, CVSS exploitability sub-score, availability of attack tooling for the relevant mobile platform), and the identity and date of the analyst performing the assessment. This supports both internal quality assurance and external assessment.

Impact records should capture: the impact dimensions assessed (e.g., data confidentiality, user safety, economic harm, accessibility), the magnitude rating assigned per dimension, the aggregation method used where multiple dimensions are affected, and any assumptions made regarding the user population or deployment context. Where CVSS v3.1 or v4.0 impact sub-scores are used as inputs, this should be noted. Documentation should be sufficient to allow a third party to reproduce or challenge the estimate. NIST SSDF RV.1.3 supports this documentation requirement.

### 4.7 Product Cybersecurity Risk Evaluation and Risk Acceptance {#s-4-7}

## Introduction

Product cybersecurity risk evaluation involves comparing identified risks against preestablished risk acceptance criteria to determine whether each risk is acceptable or requires treatment. Accepting a risk is a conscious decision to acknowledge it without taking further action to reduce it, provided it meets the predetermined criteria.

Accepted residual risks do not disappear - they are effectively shared with the product's user. This sharing is conditional: it requires that the conditions of use clearly communicate any controls or operational environment requirements needed to use the product securely. Risk sharing does not relieve a manufacturer of legal obligations, and is particularly relevant for products used as components, where certain risks cannot be addressed at the component level and instead need to be managed by the integrating party.

Output: evaluation of determined risks and justification for risk acceptance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.7-CR-01

Every identified risk shall be systematically assessed against the pre-established risk acceptance criteria to determine whether it can be accepted as-is or shall be subjected to treatment measures.

Source: RMA-06-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.7-CR-02

A risk may be deemed acceptable only when it demonstrably aligns with the predetermined risk acceptance criteria defined in 5.3. Risks that do not meet these criteria shall not be accepted, regardless of other considerations such as cost or feasibility.

Source: RMA-06-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.7-CR-03

When residual risks are shared with users - because the product relies on the operational environment or user action to provide necessary controls - it shall be verified that the required user mitigations are realistic and achievable for the intended user base, given their expected knowledge and capability. Risk acceptance under these conditions is contingent on this verification.

Source: RMA-06-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

When residual risks are shared with users - for example, because the product is intended to be deployed within a specific operational environment that provides additional controls - the manufacturer should verify that the required mitigations are realistic for the intended user base. For instance, a component lacking built-in access controls may be acceptable if the intended operational environment provides those controls externally, but this assumption needs to be clearly communicated and needs to be achievable by the expected users. Similarly, a memory chip that does not support data confidentiality or integrity may transfer that responsibility to an integrator, but only if the integrator can reasonably be expected to implement the necessary protections.

NOTE 1: Sharing risk with users does not exempt a manufacturer from its legal responsibilities.

NOTE 2: This applies particularly to products that function as components: certain risks affecting a component simply cannot be resolved at that level and are therefore passed on to whoever integrates or uses the product.

NOTE 3: In some cases it may be appropriate for the manufacturer to organize a recall of a product subject to a severe risk discovered after the product is placed on the market, where that risk cannot be addressed by action of the user.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.7-CR-04

For each accepted or residual risk, a documented acceptance justification shall be produced and retained explaining why the risk is considered acceptable. This justification shall reference the risk acceptance criteria from 5.3 and shall describe any conditions of use or operational environment assumptions on which the acceptance is predicated.

## Source:

- RMA-06-RQ-04
- 6.4.5.4 output requirement and 6.4.5.5 assessment criteria (40000-1-2)

### 4.8 Product Cybersecurity Risk Treatment {#s-4-8}

## Introduction

Risk treatment aims to reduce risks to an acceptable residual level. The primary approaches are risk avoidance - eliminating the source of a risk entirely - and risk mitigation - implementing controls that reduce likelihood or impact. Where neither is feasible within the product itself, adjusting the product context (e.g., restricting intended use or operating environment) can bring risks within acceptable bounds.

When risks cannot be fully addressed through product changes, user-side action may be necessary. In such cases, users need to be clearly informed of the remaining risks and what actions they should take. The appropriate level of information shared with users depends on their expected capabilities and context. For instance, insecure features may be disabled by default and only enabled through explicit user configuration, accompanied by clear warnings.

Output: risk treatment decisions with rationale.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.8-CR-01

For every risk that does not satisfy the established risk acceptance criteria, a treatment option that is appropriate to the product context shall be applied.

Source: RMA-07-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Risk treatment options include:

- Risk avoidance: eliminating the source of the risk altogether - for instance by removing interfaces that serve no purpose, steering clear of libraries that are not yet mature, dropping insecure legacy communication protocols, or dropping support for external plugins or scripting where it is not genuinely needed.
- Risk mitigation: implementing controls that reduce the likelihood or impact of a risk. Note that adding controls may itself introduce new risks or alter existing ones, requiring a repeat of the risk assessment.
- Context adjustment: altering the intended purpose or conditions of use to modify the risk acceptance criteria, thereby rendering a previously unacceptable risk acceptable.
- User-side treatment: where risks cannot be avoided or mitigated within the product itself, informing users of the remaining risks and the actions required of them. This is particularly relevant when insecure features need to remain available but are disabled by default, with users explicitly enabling them via configuration accompanied by clear warnings.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.8-CR-02

For each risk subject to treatment, documentation shall be made of the treatment option selected and the justification for why that option is appropriate given the product context together with the applicable risk acceptance criteria.

Source: RMA-07-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Documentation of the risk treatment decision should capture which treatment option was selected for each unacceptable risk and why that option is appropriate given the product context and risk acceptance criteria. Documentation should be sufficient to support traceability and auditability of risk management decisions. The output should include a risk treatment decision with justification per risk, and assessors will verify that the justification is aligned with the risk acceptance criteria established in 5.3.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.8-CR-03

Following the application of any risk treatment measure, the affected risks shall be reevaluated to determine whether residual risks indeed meet the established acceptance criteria.

Source: RMA-07-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Re-evaluation should account for the fact that risk treatment measures - particularly mitigation controls - can change the profile of existing risks and may introduce new risks. The re-evaluation feeds back into the risk assessment process (see 5.5 - 5.7), ensuring that residual risks are measured against the established acceptance criteria. This iterative cycle continues until all risks are either acceptable or have been addressed through an appropriate treatment option.

### 4.9 Product Cybersecurity Risk Communication {#s-4-9}

## Introduction

Risk communication ensures that users receive clear, actionable information about cybersecurity risks associated with a product. This includes both the risks transferred to the user and the measures users are expected to take to mitigate them. Communication should be tailored to the needs of the intended audience: while technical language may suffice when addressing other manufacturers, end users - including those with impairments - may require simpler language or alternative formats to meaningfully access and act on this information.

Output: documentation containing the circumstances and misuse that can lead to significant cybersecurity risks, conditions of use, and mitigation instructions to users.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.9-CR-01

Risk communication directed at users shall employ language and methods appropriate to the audience; where the audience consists of consumers, the language used shall be clear and free of technical jargon to the extent practicable.

Source: RMA-08-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance:

When communicating risks to end users, avoid jargon and technical terminology. Consider the audience's background and adjust the language accordingly. For instance, a consumer product manual should describe risks and mitigations in plain language, whereas documentation directed at professional integrators or other manufacturers may use more technical terms where mutually understood.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.9-CR-02

Where a product is subject to applicable accessibility obligations or where the intended user base includes individuals with impairments, risk communication shall consider formats and using language to ensure each user can meaningfully access the information.

Source: RMA-08-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Where a product is subject to accessibility legislation (e.g. the European Accessibility Act), or where the user base is known to include individuals with impairments, risk communication should be made available in multiple formats. Examples include audio descriptions, screenreader-compatible digital documents, or printed materials with simplified language. Relying solely on a website for risk disclosure may be insufficient for users without reliable internet access or those with visual impairments.

NOTE: What counts as adequate communication depends on who the audience is. Some end users may be unable to access written information at all or may be excluded if that information exists only on a website. Where the recipient is another manufacturer, however, simply providing the information in a language they understand may be enough.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.9-CR-03

Risk communication documentation shall address a minimum set of elements: the circumstances and foreseeable misuse scenarios that could give rise to significant cybersecurity risks; the mitigation measures users are expected to implement; and the operational conditions under which the product may be used securely.

Source: RMA-08-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Risk communication documentation should cover:

1. Scenarios in which the product could be misused or exposed to elevated risk, including foreseeable misuse cases identified during risk assessment;
2. Concrete steps users can take to reduce those risks, such as network segmentation, configuration hardening, or restricted physical access; and
3. The operational conditions under which the product can be considered secure, for example supported software versions, required network configurations, or maintenance obligations.

### 4.10 Product Cybersecurity Risk Review {#s-4-10}

Introduction

Maintaining appropriate cybersecurity over a product's lifetime requires periodic review and, where necessary, updating of risk management activities to account for changes in the threat landscape and the evolving state of the art. Reviews may be conducted at regular intervals, with the frequency determined by the nature of the risks and the specific product context.

Output: record of the review and any updates to risk management documentation.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.10-CR-01

Reviews of product cybersecurity risk management activities shall be conducted at planned intervals, where the frequency of those intervals is determined by the risk assessment and the context in which the product operates, and at least once a year - despite design staying the same.

Source: RMA-09-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

The appropriate interval between reviews is not fixed; it should be calibrated to the risk level and the context in which the product operates. Higher-risk products or those deployed in rapidly changing environments may warrant more frequent reviews.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.10-CR-02

In addition to planned-interval reviews, a review of risk management activities shall be initiated when trigger conditions are met, including product modification, context changes, changes to risk acceptance criteria, changes in cybersecurity risk exposure (including threat landscape changes), identification of a known exploitable vulnerability, occurrence of a severe incident, or obsolescence of a component with cybersecurity impact.

Source: RMA-09-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Beyond planned interval reviews, organizations should establish monitoring mechanisms capable of detecting these trigger conditions in a timely manner. This may include subscribing to threat and vulnerability intelligence feeds and tracking cybersecurity testing outcomes so that event-driven reviews can be initiated promptly when a trigger is identified.

## Requirement CR-ID: 5.10-CR-03

Where a review conducted under 5.10-CR-01 or 5.10-CR-02 reveals that existing risk assessment documentation is affected, the relevant documentation produced under Clause 5 shall be updated accordingly.

Source: RMA-09-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Updating documentation may include adding or modifying product controls where the review reveals that existing controls are insufficient to address newly identified or changed risks.

## 5 Product Cybersecurity Lifecycle Activities {#s-5}

### 5.1 Introduction {#s-5-1}

Cybersecurity lifecycle activities for mobile applications and their backend services are intended to integrate with modern software development practices, including agile and DevSecOps approaches, rather than depend on a single linear process. Although some activities require prerequisite inputs, many can be performed concurrently or in varying sequences. Additionally, activities may be revisited at appropriate points or at regular intervals, as a change in one activity can have implications for several others.

### 5.2 Product Cybersecurity Planning {#s-5-2}

## Introduction

Product cybersecurity planning defines the cybersecurity activities applicable to a product throughout its lifecycle. The extent and frequency of these activities are informed by the risks identified through risk assessment, for example when determining the type or cadence of testing to be performed. Although the activities are generally consistent across development approaches, the way they are carried out may differ. Planning typically produces a living document that is updated as further information becomes available and may refer to organization-wide policies where activities are implemented consistently across multiple products.

Output: Documented product cybersecurity planning.

See OpenCRE 635-851 at opencre.org/cre/635-851 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.2-CR-01

The product cybersecurity plan shall take the product context from 5.2 into account, when available, and define, at minimum, every applicable cybersecurity activity defined in Clauses 6 and 7.

## Source:

- CLA-01-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)
- SOTA

## Guidance

Certain activities may be organization-wide instead of just for the product, in which case the plan can reference an organization-wide policy.

Mobile application development introduces platform-specific lifecycle phases and artefacts (e.g., app store submission, OS version compatibility cycles, SDK dependency updates) that differ from generic software development. The planning procedure should identify which activities apply per platform and per lifecycle phase.

Mobile application development teams frequently include platform-specific engineers, backend engineers responsible for RDPS, and release managers handling app store submissions, each with distinct security responsibilities. The plan can assign named roles or role types to planned cybersecurity activities and consider proper training for the people involved.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.2-CR-02

Throughout the entire product lifecycle, the product cybersecurity plan shall be kept current through regular maintenance and review, and the execution of all planned activities shall be actively tracked. Review shall take place not only on a regular schedule but also upon occurrence of defined triggers.

## Source:

- CLA-01-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)
- SOTA (triggers)

## Guidance

The product cybersecurity plan should be treated as a document that develops over time. It may start with limited detail and be expanded as further information becomes available. Reviews should take into account changes in the risk landscape, such as newly discovered threats after release that may require adjustments to planned testing. Monitoring progress against the plan helps confirm that agreed activities are performed and that missing or delayed actions are detected early. The plan may also address roles, responsibilities, and training needs, so that cybersecurity activities can be maintained throughout the product lifecycle.

### 5.3 Product Cybersecurity Requirements {#s-5-3}

## Introduction

Product cybersecurity requirements specify what shall be implemented in the product. They are grounded in the product context, informed by risk assessment, and shaped first by applicable legal and regulatory obligations, then by stakeholder needs. In defining these requirements, qualities such as traceability, validity, understandability, and verifiability are typically considered, together with the cybersecurity characteristics of the product’s operating environment across its lifecycle, including development, deployment, production, maintenance, and decommissioning. These requirements provide a foundation for subsequent engineering activities and should be actively managed throughout the product lifecycle.

Output: Documented cybersecurity requirements.

See OpenCRE 004-517 at opencre.org/cre/004-517 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.3-CR-01

Product cybersecurity requirements shall be derived from and grounded in the product context, the decisions made regarding treatment of product cybersecurity risks, and all applicable regulatory requirements.

Source: CLA-02-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

When specifying product cybersecurity requirements, consider ensuring they are traceable back to their source inputs (product context, risk treatment decisions, regulatory requirements, stakeholder needs), understandable to relevant stakeholders, and verifiable through assessment or testing. Requirements should reflect the cybersecurity properties needed across the product's environment during development, deployment, production, maintenance, and decommissioning.

For mobile applications, requirements should account for platform-specific threat surfaces (iOS, Android, cross-platform frameworks) and the cybersecurity properties of any Remote Data Processing Solutions (RDPS) the application depends upon.

NIST SSDF practice PO.1 ("Define Security Requirements for Software Development") and OWASP MASVS provide relevant reference points for structuring mobile-specific security requirement sets.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.3-CR-02

Whenever any of the defined inputs - product context, risk assessment outcomes, risk treatment decisions, or applicable regulatory requirements - undergo change, the product cybersecurity requirements shall be reviewed and updated as necessary to remain current and accurate.

## Source:

- CLA-02-RQ-02;
- input list from section 7.3.2 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Organizations may consider establishing a change management process or trigger-based review mechanism to ensure that updates to any of these inputs are systematically evaluated for their impact on the product cybersecurity requirements.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.3-CR-03

Changes to product cybersecurity requirements shall be communicated to all affected development, testing, and operations teams in a timely and documented manner, with impact assessment by each affected party.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Communication may be formalized through a requirements change notification process integrated into the project's change control board or sprint planning cycle. For mobile applications developed using agile or DevSecOps methods, requirement changes should be reflected in the product backlog with security impact labels, and downstream artefacts (threat models, test plans, security test cases) should be flagged for update.

### 5.4 Cybersecurity Architecture and Design {#s-5-4}

## Introduction

Cybersecurity architecture and design translate the cybersecurity requirements (defined in 6.3) and product context (defined in 5.2) into concrete design decisions and control selections. Design decisions are based on those requirements and may, where necessary, result in refinement of the cybersecurity requirements. Key design considerations include defining trust boundaries between components and subsystems, designing secure interfaces with attention to authentication, input validation, and attack surface minimization, and ensuring secure-by-default configurations. Typical design artefacts include design documents, interface definitions, and data-flow or trust-boundary diagrams. Catalogues such as draft prEN 40000-1-4 or vertical standards under standardization request M/606 may serve as reference sources for control selection, though manufacturers are free to use other technically appropriate sources.

Output: Documented cybersecurity architecture and design.

See OpenCRE 326-704 at opencre.org/cre/326-704 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.4-CR-01

A specification of the product's cybersecurity architecture and design shall be produced. This specification shall include the selection of cybersecurity controls chosen to satisfy the cybersecurity requirements established in 6.3.

Source: CLA-03-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

The cybersecurity architecture and design documentation can, where relevant, describe how the product is structured and protected. This may cover default security configurations for components, the product’s internal and external interfaces and the protections applied to them, and diagrams that show data flows, trust boundaries, components, and subsystems.

The choice of controls can be based on suitable control catalogues, such as EN 40000-1-4, relevant sector-specific standards developed under standardization request M/606, or other sources that are technically appropriate for the product and its risks.

### 5.5 Secure Implementation {#s-5-5}

## Introduction

Secure implementation ensures that a product is built in accordance with its cybersecurity requirements and architecture.

Output:

- documentation on securing the development environment;
- the product with implemented cybersecurity according to security requirements, secure coding standard, architecture and design, and approved cryptography, including secure hardware modules;
- secure coding standard;
- documented process regarding memory-unsafe programming;
- documented process for managing keys and certificates;
- documented protocol inventory review;
- documented compensating security for vulnerable protocols;

- documented changes to risk management and lifecycle, if any, caused by implementation deviations.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-01

The product shall be developed and maintained securely by using a secure development environment to prevent unauthorized access, to an extent appropriate given the product's risk profile, design, and scope. This shall be demonstrated by including the development environment in the scope of the provider’s Information Security Management System certified against ISO/IEC 27001 by an accredited certification body.

Source: CLA-04-RQ-01(40000-1-2), SOTA (27001 for this security level)

## Guidance

A secure development environment may include measures such as:

- access control and monitoring of access to engineer workstations, source code repositories, build systems, components, signing infrastructure, provisioning profiles, and CI/CD pipelines;
- branch protection rules;
- separation of development, build, test, and production environments;
- patching and hardening of development systems;
- protection of secrets, keys, and credentials used in development;
- development environments monitoring for suspicious activity;
- controls over who may trigger production builds or submit applications to app stores (Google Play, Apple App Store).

See OpenCRE 148-853 at opencre.org/cre/148-853 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-02

The product shall implement all cybersecurity requirements established in 6.3, in conformance with the cybersecurity architecture and design defined in 6.4.

Source: CLA-04-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Implementation should include the cybersecurity controls defined during design.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-03

A documented secure coding standard shall be adopted and enforced, applicable to the programming languages and frameworks used in the mobile application, covering at minimum: prohibited functions, memory safety practices, input validation, output encoding, error handling, preventing common security weaknesses, and prohibition of hard-coded credentials.

Source: SOTA and guidance

## Guidance

Coding standards support code quality, consistency, and avoiding weaknesses.

Applicable sources may include the CERT Secure Coding Standards (SEI CERT C, C++, Java), OWASP Mobile Top 10, and platform-specific guidance from Google (Android Developers Security) and Apple. For cross-platform frameworks (React Native, Flutter), the standard should address framework-specific risks. The standard should be enforced through automated static analysis and linting integrated into the CI/CD, and be the input for code review.

See OpenCRE 036-275 at opencre.org/cre/036-275 for related resources and topics for guidance, and for an overview of all technical application security controls: opencre.org/cre/636-660

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-04

A process shall be established for identifying, reviewing, and approving the use of memoryunsafe programming languages or constructs in the mobile application, and shall document the rationale and compensating controls where their use cannot be avoided.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Where native code (C/C++) is used in Android NDK modules or iOS frameworks, memorysafe practices should be applied including bounds checking, use of safe string and memory functions, and static analysis for buffer overflows and use-after-free vulnerabilities. Consider migration to memory-safe languages (Rust, Swift, Kotlin) where feasible.

The guidance "The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps" (2023) by CISA, NSA et al provides a roadmap approach.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-05

Where secure implementation activities produce deviations from the cybersecurity architecture and design, reviews shall be triggered of the cybersecurity risk management activities, as defined in 5.10 and all affected cybersecurity product lifecycle activities.

Source: CLA-04-RQ-06 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Deviations can occur when practical implementation limits, selected tools, or the behaviour of components do not match the assumptions made during design. When this happens, the architecture and design documentation should be reviewed and updated where needed. The product cybersecurity requirements and related risk management activities should also be reconsidered, so that the product’s security position remains aligned with the intended design.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-06

The product shall use cryptographic mechanisms that reflect the state of the art and that conform to the cryptographic requirements applicable to the product and agreed within its certification, regulatory, or sectoral context - covering the selection of algorithms, parameters, key sizes, operational modes, random number generation, key lifecycle management, and the deprecation policy.

Where the applicable requirements do not designate a specific cryptographic reference, the agreed cryptographic mechanisms defined in the ECCG “Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms” (ACM) shall be used as the recognised baseline. Where the product is subject to a European Digital Identity Wallet certification scheme or to the EUCC, the applicable ACM version is the one required by that scheme (via the EUCC “Guidelines on Cryptography”) at the time of the conformity assessment or surveillance evaluation; versions issued as drafts or for public review are excluded until adopted.

Where the applicable requirements or the ACM do not address a specific mechanism, equivalent state-of-the-art cryptographic guidance shall be applied. Continued conformity as the applicable requirements or the applicable ACM version evolve shall be maintained in accordance with 6.5-CR-09.

## Source:

- REQ-CON-002 (40000-10)
- SOTA (fallback obligation; alignment of the applicable requirements and version with the product’s certification/regulatory context)

## Guidance:

The requirement is deliberately layered. The primary obligation is to meet the cryptographic requirements that are applicable to the product and agreed within its context, while reflecting the state of the art; the ECCG “Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms” (ACM) is then named as the concrete reference. This keeps the requirement usable both for products inside a formal certification scheme and for high-attack-potential mobile applications addressed under other regimes.

Determining what is applicable and agreed depends on the product's context. For a product certified under, or being prepared for, a European Digital Identity Wallet certification scheme (built on the EUCC), the applicable agreed reference is the ECCG/ENISA ACM in the version the scheme mandates at the time of assessment. This mirrors how the EU framework itself handles the reference: the ACM version is carried in a maintained companion document (the EUCC “Guidelines on Cryptography”).

For other mobile applications exposed to adversaries with a high attack potential, the applicable requirements may come from a sectoral scheme, a regulatory regime, or a customer or contractual security baseline. Where one of these designates a cryptographic reference, that reference governs; where none does, the ACM serves as the recognized default baseline, because it expresses mechanisms agreed as state of the art across the EU national cybersecurity certification authorities.

At the time of writing, the current ACM version is v2 (May 2025). A version 3, realigned for the post-quantum era, was in public review until the end of July 2026; once adopted and taken up by the applicable scheme or baseline, it becomes the applicable version and the migration provisions of 6.5-CR-09 apply. Manufacturers should confirm the version and any cryptographic reference mandated by their specific context, since these can be updated independently of this document. Drafts and public-review versions are not applicable until adopted; the intent is a deferred-dated reference in which the applicable context fixes a single version at any point in time, giving a determinate target while allowing the baseline to advance without amending this document.

Because high-attack-potential contexts (and, for wallets, Level of Assurance High) demand a current cryptographic baseline and a credible post-quantum path, the product should be designed for cryptographic agility, so that algorithms and parameters can be replaced — including migration to post-quantum or hybrid mechanisms — during the product's lifecycle and support period without redesign. Note that the ACM sets validity periods and deprecation deadlines for legacy mechanisms; migration timing may be dictated by those deadlines rather than by a fixed interval.

See OpenCRE 170-772 at opencre.org/cre/170-772 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-07

The product shall protect cryptographic keys through secure hardware modules. If hardwarebased protection is not feasible, the product shall use secure software modules to protect cryptographic keys.

Source: REQ-CON-003 (40000-10)

## Guidance

Cryptographic keys play a central role in protecting the product, its communications, and its data. They should therefore be stored using strong protection measures. Where suitable for the product, hardware-based protection such as hardware security modules, or comparable trusted execution environments, should be used.

If hardware-based protection is not suitable because of the product’s design or practical constraints, software-based measures, such as encrypted key stores or secure enclaves, may be used as an alternative.

See OpenCRE 032-213 at opencre.org/cre/032-213 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-08

A process shall be established for inventorying and verifying all locations in the mobile application and its RDPS where cryptographic keys are generated, stored, used, and destroyed. Verification shall ensure that each location meets the cryptographic requirements in this document.

Source: SOTA

## Guidance

The inventory should cover: keys stored in the Android Keystore system or iOS Secure Enclave/Keychain; keys used in RDPS backend services; keys embedded in configuration files or transmitted over the network; and keys used by third-party SDKs. For each key, document: the key type and purpose, the protection mechanism applied, the hardware backing status (e.g., StrongBox on Android, Secure Enclave on iOS), and the key lifecycle.

OWASP MASVS-CRYPTO-1/-2 and OWASP MASTG provide test cases for verifying key protection. Align with NIST SSDF PW.5.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-09

A process shall be established for periodically reviewing the protocol inventory (see technical documentation in 6.6) against current state-of-the-art guidance and for identifying protocols that have been deprecated, are vulnerable, or require compensating measures in accordance with 6.5-CR-10.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

The review should be triggered by: publication of new vulnerability disclosures affecting protocols or mechanisms in the inventory; a change to the applicable cryptographic requirements or the adoption of a new applicable ACM version (or other state-of-the-art guidance) that deprecates algorithms, parameters, protocol versions, or cipher suites; and at defined periodic intervals (at least annually). For mobile applications, particular attention should be paid to TLS version support across the range of OS versions the application supports, as older OS versions may not support current TLS configurations.

Where the product is certified, aligning the transition period with the scheme's own maintenance mechanisms - such as mandatory surveillance evaluations under a wallet certification regime, and the assurance-continuity handling of updated state-of-the-art documents under EUCC - keeps the certified status consistent as the cryptographic baseline evolves and avoids the product silently falling out of conformity between assessments. Where the product is not certified, the same review-and-migrate discipline should be applied against the applicable baseline. The review outcome should feed into the vulnerability management process and, where protocol or mechanism changes are required, into the deviation handling process under 6.5-CR-05.

Align with OWASP MASVS-NETWORK and NIST SSDF RV.1.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.5-CR-10

When the product relies on legacy or vulnerable protocols, the product shall implement security measures mitigating protocol issues - such as, but not limited to, multi-factor authentication - sufficient to maintain a security level commensurate with the risks introduced by those protocols.

Source: REQ-EMM-002 (40000-10)

## Guidance

Use the protocol inventory maintained under 6.6-CR-04 to determine whether any outdated or vulnerable protocols are still used by the product.

Where such protocols cannot be avoided, additional protections should be applied. These may include measures such as multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, access control lists, stronger monitoring, or encryption layers around the communication.

Some weaker protocols may be needed to remain compatible with older systems or products. However, their use should not lower the product’s overall cybersecurity level. The added protections should be appropriate to the risk created by the specific protocol.

### 5.6 Technical Product Documentation {#s-5-6}

## Introduction

Technical product documentation extends product context documentation with technical details.

Output:

- a list of integrated components;

- documentation on complying with components' intended purpose and instructions;
- technical documentation and user information and instructions;

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.6-CR-01

The product shall maintain an identified list of all integrated components including at least the top-level dependencies and the transitive dependencies when technically feasible, in a commonly used machine-readable format. This is referred to as an SBOM (Software Bill Of Materials). A list entry shall include the type of dependency, software producer, unique component identifier (e.g. producer, component name, and component version). The SBOM shall contain the identity of the SBOM author, a version indicator, and a timestamp. When integrating third-party components, the intended purpose and user instructions to address cybersecurity risks of those components are the conditions that shall be adhered to.

## Source:

- (40000-1-2) CLA-04-RQ-03; CLA-04-RQ-04
- (40000-1-3) PRE-7-RQ-01 (SBOM); PRE-7-RQ-02 (SBOM content); PRE-7-RQ-03(top level); PRE-7-RQ-04(format); PRE-7-RQ-06 (metadata); PRE-7-RQ-03-RE (transitive); PRE-7-RQ-07 (required information); PRE-1-RQ-04 (SBOM for vulnerability handling)

## Guidance:

When a vulnerability is disclosed in third-party or open-source software, organizations need to quickly determine whether the affected component is present in their products. That requires an accurate record of the software components included in each product, along with their origins, dependencies, and supporting documentation.

The identification process should make use of all available relevant inputs - including source code, binary artefacts, configuration files, and cybersecurity architecture documentation - to achieve a complete picture. The intended outcome is a thorough, traceable inventory of components that can underpin vulnerability assessments across the full product lifecycle.

Top-level dependencies are components that are directly incorporated into or required by the product. Further clarification on how to define and scope top-level dependencies can be found in BSI TR-03183-2 v2.1.0, section 8.3.1.

Capturing transitive dependencies - those that are indirectly required through other components - in the SBOM supports quicker and more effective identification of vulnerabilities that may be inherited from upstream components. It is recognized that complete enumeration of transitive dependencies may not always be achievable, as suppliers do not always provide the information needed. For further guidance on scoping the depth and breadth of SBOM content, ISO/IEC 27036-3:2023, Annex B, section B.3.1.3 is a relevant reference.

Among the machine-readable formats widely used in the software industry, SPDX (standardized as ISO/IEC 5962:2021) and CycloneDX are commonly adopted options.

Where an open-source component is maintained under the oversight of an open-source steward, the stewarding organization's name should be entered in the software producer field.

Unique component identifiers function as reference keys that allow components to be looked up in vulnerability databases. Recognized identifier types include Common Platform Enumeration (CPE), Package URL (PURL), and SoftWare Hash IDentifier (SWHID); where multiple identifiers exist for a component, all may be recorded.
