Licence information is an optional supplementary field that may also be captured for each component.

When third-party libraries are selected and integrated, preference should be given to libraries that are secure, actively maintained, and kept current. Integrated components should also be configured carefully, because configuration choices and implementation options can influence the cybersecurity of the product as a whole.

See OpenCRE 863-521 at opencre.org/cre/863-521 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.6-CR-02

A mapping of upstream dependencies and interdependencies, apart from components, shall be available to support coordination and notification when a vulnerability is discovered, so that related issues can be resolved without undue delay.

In case the application employs AI models, any externally supplied element for this employment shall be part of this mapping, including third-party models, training data, augmentation data, MCP servers and agentic skills.

## Source:

- PRE-1-RQ-04 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (AI)

## Guidance

When a vulnerability is identified, this inventory, next to an SBOM, supports the rapid identification of affected elements and facilitates timely engagement with the relevant upstream stakeholders.

More guidance regarding AI-dependencies and AIBOM (AI Bill Of Materials) can be found in ISO/IEC 27090, prEN18282, and the OWASP AI Exchange as it is designed to represent the consensus of these standards.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.6-CR-03

If a new software build or release is created, or if an inaccuracy is found in the current SBOM, a revised SBOM shall be issued.

## Source:

- PRE-7-RQ-05 (40000-1-3)
- PRE-7-RC-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance:

The obligation to produce a new SBOM extends beyond major or feature releases and applies to any build that incorporates an updated component or dependency, regardless of whether other aspects of the product have changed. This includes dependency changes introduced through automated dependency management tools such as Dependabot or Renovate. To ensure SBOM currency is maintained independently of feature release cycles, organizations should establish procedures that trigger SBOM regeneration as part of the pull request or merge workflow whenever such updates occur.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.6-CR-04

Technical documentation and user instructions shall be written in language easily understood by the user and shall include at least:

- a) documentation of all logical and physical interfaces and transport protocols with their security properties;
- b) cybersecurity prerequisites for the deployment environment;
- c) a description of implemented security functions;
- d) usage instructions covering installation and hardening;
- e) data deletion and decommissioning procedures; and
- f) detailed configuration and maintenance instructions.

These topics shall at least cover when applicable: configuration baselines, safe defaults, backup and restore, patching and updating, key rotation, log management including synchronization of time, incident response hooks, and interactions with platform security services (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore, biometric APIs, app sandboxing).

## Source:

- CLA-04-RQ-05 (40000-1-2)
- REQ-TGSA-003 [sub-item (a)] (40000-10)
- REQ-KEV-003 [sub-item (b)] (40000-10)
- REQ-SBD-001 [sub-item (c)] (40000-10)
- REQ-DRT-002 [content specification for sub-item (d)] (40000-10)
- REQ-DRT-003 [sub-item (e)] (40000-10)
- REQ-DRT-004 [content specification for sub-item (f)] (40000-10)
- SOTA (interactions with platform security services)

## Guidance

Technical documentation and user instructions may be prepared and updated at various phases of the product lifecycle. Regardless of when they are drafted, they should be reviewed for consistency and appropriateness, typically during verification and validation activities.

- a) For sub-item (a): Enumerate every physical and logical interface and protocol the product uses. For each one, capture relevant security properties (e.g. authentication, confidentiality, integrity), any trust boundaries involved, and whether it is enabled by default or optional, together with the protocol version, cipher policy, and any relevant state-of-the-art conformity or certification. Because interfaces and protocols are frequently targeted by attackers, documenting them thoroughly helps ensure they are configured and tested correctly.
- b) For sub-item (b): Specify OS and hypervisor versions, database hardening requirements, PKI requirements, network segmentation and ACLs, and SIEM integration requirements. This enables avoidance of deploying a securely designed product on an information system that does not meet the necessary requirements.
- c) For sub-item (c): Document the product's security functions, which may include (among others) authentication, authorization, logging, secure update, secure boot, rate limiting, secure storage at both the physical and logical level, physical protection, safeguards against sensitive-data exposure via the user interface (e.g. clipboard, screenshots, app-switcher snapshots, keyboard caching), and any accepted residual risk. Setting these functions out explicitly turns the product's

protection goals into something that can be checked and tested. Cryptographic functions should be documented as described under 6.6-CR-05.

- d) For sub-item (d): Set out the instructions end users need to operate the product, covering secure installation, initial hardening, account management, backup and restore, safe default settings, and warning banners. Together these give the end user everything they need to use the product correctly.
- e) For sub-item (e): Explain the procedures available to the user for a factory reset, for purging selected data, and, where supported, for cryptographic erasure, including how to verify each of these completed successfully. Clear data-deletion instructions are needed both to meet privacy obligations and to support proper decommissioning of the product.
- f) For sub-item (f): Supply configuration baselines together with the procedures for patching, updating, rotating keys, managing logs, taking backups, hooking into incident response, and synchronizing time. Taken together, this equips administrators with everything they need to keep the product running securely.

Documentation should describe how the mobile application uses platform-provided security primitives, the trust model between the application and its RDPS, and the security assumptions made about the underlying mobile operating system version. This documentation supports both internal security review and external assessment. OWASP MASVS-STORAGE and OWASP MASVS-CRYPTO provide a framework for what platform security service usage should be documented. OWASP MASTG provides test cases that can be cross-referenced against this documentation.

The protocol inventory should cover: application-layer protocols (HTTP/S, WebSocket, MQTT, gRPC, custom binary protocols); transport-layer protocols and versions (TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3); authentication protocols (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML); and any legacy or proprietary protocols. For each protocol, document: the version in use, the security properties applied (authentication, confidentiality, integrity), the cipher suites or algorithm parameters, and whether the protocol is enabled by default or optionally. Third-party SDKs often introduce undocumented protocol usage; static and dynamic analysis tools (OWASP MASTG network testing techniques) should be used to detect these. Align with OWASP MASVS-NETWORK.

Where TLS is used for sensitive communications, the inventory should also record whether certificate or public-key pinning is applied and, if so, the pinning and key-rotation strategy, given the operational trade-off between resistance to interception and the risk of denial of service if pinned keys are rotated without a corresponding application update.

See OpenCRE 820-877 at opencre.org/cre/820-877 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.6-CR-05

The product's technical documentation shall provide a detailed specification of all cryptographic mechanisms employed, including the algorithms used, their parameters, key sizes, operational modes, random generation methods, key lifecycle management, and policy of deprecation.

Source: REQ-CON-001(40000-10)

## Guidance

The cryptographic specification should describe the cryptographic mechanisms used in the product in enough detail to support conformity checks and evaluation of the product’s security position.

The specification should also link to the security functions documented under 6.6-CR-04(c), where those functions rely on cryptography.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.6-CR-06

The product's technical documentation shall include an artefact - such as a coverage matrix - that explicitly links each identified risk to the security function or functions that address it.

Source: REQ-SBD-002 (40000-10)

## Guidance

A matrix or equivalent structured artefact should be provided within the technical documentation, linking identified threats to the security functions implemented in the product, and indicating the degree of coverage for each threat. Maintaining such a coverage mapping prevents gaps in threat coverage.

NOTE: This requirement addresses the forward-looking demonstration of threat coverage within the product's technical documentation. It is distinct from the justification of accepted residual risks required by 5.7-CR-04, which concerns post-evaluation documentation of acceptance decisions. Both obligations apply and are complementary.

### 5.7 Cybersecurity Verification and Validation {#s-5-7}

## Introduction

Cybersecurity Verification and Validation (V&V) confirms that a product's concept, design, and implementation meet every applicable cybersecurity requirement and that the controls put in place actually work. Rather than being a one-off check at the end of development, it recurs across the whole product lifecycle and is generally carried out again whenever the product is modified - for instance during maintenance work or once a newly found vulnerability has been resolved.

A range of testing techniques may be applied depending on the product's risk and design: functional, unit, integration, system, fuzz, stress, and penetration testing each address distinct aspects of security.

Output: Documentation of selected verification and validation approaches and their outcome.

See OpenCRE 433-442 at opencre.org/cre/433-442 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-01

Verification and validation shall take key elements as input:

- the product implementation including relevant hardware, software, and remote data processing solutions;
- the technical documentation, together with user information and instructions;
- the cybersecurity requirements;
- the product cybersecurity context including relevant information about use from for example customer input and support cases;

- the cybersecurity state-of-the art as described in publications, standards, and guidelines;
- the evolving threat landscape applicable to the product, including information on vulnerabilities found in similar products including components.

## Source:

- Input clause 7.6 (40000-1-2)
- PRE-9-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-02

The cybersecurity verification and validation process shall confirm that the product is sufficiently secure, meaning it satisfies the cybersecurity requirements established in 6.3 and the levels of the identified risks (see 5.5) meet the acceptance criteria (see 5.3).

## Source:

- CLA-05-RQ-01 (40000-1-2) - but the subject is scoped from the security controls to the product
- CLA-05-RQ-02 (40000-1-2) – further specifying the role of risk assessment

## Guidance

Cybersecurity analysis methods can be used to review implementation artefacts and check whether the intended cybersecurity controls have been implemented correctly and fully. These methods may include static and dynamic analysis, inspections, and peer reviews.

Functional testing can also be used to verify that the implemented product behaviour matches the defined cybersecurity requirements.

Traceability between cybersecurity requirements, implemented controls, and corresponding test cases can be maintained in a requirements traceability matrix (RTM) or equivalent artefact.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-03

Threat scenarios and attack profiles shall be defined, documented, and used as the basis for validation testing, derived from the applicable attack potential level (e.g., AVA\_VAN level), the risk assessment and the product's cybersecurity context . Each validation testing cycle, these shall be reviewed.

The validation testing shall include advanced penetration testing calibrated to the goal, and specialized techniques - including where applicable protocol robustness testing, deep fuzzing, verification of hardened configurations, testing of secure boot/attestation, assessment of hardware key protection, and verifying supply chain integrity.

A process for conducting these penetration tests shall be defined including: the scope of testing (including the mobile client, associated RDPS, and communication channels), the minimum qualifications required of testers, the testing methodology to be followed, and the criteria for determining when re-testing is required following remediation.

## Source:

- CLA-05-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)
- REQ-KEV-009 (40000-10)
- SOTA

## Guidance

Penetration testing - involving purposeful attacks with varying levels of pre-existing knowledge - can provide evidence that the product can withstand threats identified in the risk assessment.

Threat scenarios used for validation should reflect the operational environment of the mobile application, including threats specific to mobile platforms such as malicious applications on the same device, rooted or jailbroken device environments, network-level adversaries (e.g., on untrusted Wi-Fi), physical device access, and abuse of platform inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms.

The OWASP MASTG provides mobile-specific test scenarios that can be used to populate or cross-check the threat scenario inventory. For RDPS (remote data processing solutions) used by the mobile application, threat scenarios should additionally address server-side attack surfaces exposed via the mobile client. Scenarios should be reviewed and updated whenever the risk assessment is revised or new attack techniques relevant to the product's context are identified.

The penetration testing methodology should address mobile-specific attack surfaces such as defined in the OWASP MASTG, including but not limited to: local data storage security, interprocess communication (including URL scheme and deep link handling, and verification of Android App Links / iOS Universal Links), WebView security, binary protections, network communication, and authentication mechanisms. For RDPS, the methodology should additionally address API security testing (e.g., authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limiting). Testers should demonstrate familiarity with both iOS and Android platform security models, as applicable. Re-testing criteria should specify that all findings rated high or critical need to be re-tested after remediation before release. The organization should retain penetration test reports as evidence of V&V activities.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-04

The V&V process shall validate that all cybersecurity risks associated with integrated components - including third-party software - have been identified and adequately addressed in the product's implemented design.

Source: CLA-05-RQ-05 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Vulnerability scanning of third-party and integrated software components can help identify known vulnerabilities. Integration testing can further verify that the interaction between components does not introduce cybersecurity gaps that were not addressed during design.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-05

A process shall be established for assessing supply chain integrity as part of cybersecurity V&V, including verification that the application binary and its dependencies are built from verified sources, that the build pipeline is protected against tampering, and that the deployed artefact matches the verified build output.

Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Supply chain integrity assessment should include: verification that all source code and thirdparty dependencies are obtained from authenticated and integrity-verified sources (e.g., via cryptographic hash verification or signed package repositories); verification that the build pipeline (CI/CD system) is protected against unauthorized modification (e.g., through access controls, audit logging, and pipeline configuration management); and verification that the application binary delivered to end users (via the app store or enterprise distribution) matches the binary produced by the verified build pipeline (e.g., via reproducible builds or post-build hash comparison). For Android applications, the organization should verify that the application signing key is protected in accordance with Google Play signing requirements or equivalent. For iOS applications, the organization should verify that code signing certificates and provisioning profiles are managed securely.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-06

Where appropriate to the product's design, risk assessment, and cybersecurity context, the V&V process shall encompass key elements: artefact analysis including architecture review, error-handling and input validation, external interface and protocol assessment (including deprecation and encryption/integrity checks), additional security testing, documentation review, and risk treatment alignment verification. See guidance for these key elements.

## Source:

- CLA-05-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)
- REQ-EMM-001 (40000-10)
- SOTA

## Guidance

- Artefact analysis (a): Both manual review and automated tools (e.g., static analysis) can be applied in analysis to confirm fulfilment of cybersecurity requirements. Artefacts include code, configuration, and architecture documentation

.

- Error handling and input validation (b): Fuzz testing - subjecting the product to unexpected, random, or invalid inputs - can reveal crashes, memory leaks, or unexpected behaviour caused by inadequate input handling.
- External interfaces and protocols (c): Integration testing can identify cybersecurity gaps arising from component interactions. For protocol assessment, retrieve the protocol inventory identified in accordance with CR-ID: 6.6-CR-04. Check that none of the protocols in use is deprecated or known to be vulnerable. Confirm that each protocol provides secure transmission, including encryption and integrity checks. Vulnerability scanning tools can assist in detecting known protocol weaknesses. For RDPS APIs, the assessment should additionally verify authentication token handling, input validation at API boundaries, and correct implementation of authorization controls
- Additional security testing (d): Running dynamic testing tools, penetration testing and stress testing (to surface denial-of-service vulnerabilities or inefficient resource handling) are applicable techniques.
- Documentation review (e): A test strategy document covering what, when, and how to test can serve as a basis for assessing accuracy and completeness of cybersecurity documentation.
- Risk treatment alignment (f): Traceability between identified risks, their treatments, the implemented cybersecurity requirements, and the verification thereof should be established and verified.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-07

A process shall be established for selecting, configuring, and maintaining static application security testing (SAST) tools and dynamic application security testing (DAST) tools appropriate for the mobile platform(s) in scope (iOS, Android, or cross-platform), and the rationale for tool selection relative to the product's technology stack and cybersecurity requirements shall be documented.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

For Android applications, SAST tools may need to be capable of analyzing Java/Kotlin bytecode and native code (e.g., via APK analysis). For iOS applications, tools may need to support analysis of Swift and Objective-C source and binaries. For cross-platform frameworks (e.g., React Native, Flutter), the organization should ideally confirm that selected tools cover both the framework layer and the underlying platform code. Tool configurations should be reviewed at least annually and upon significant changes to the technology stack.

The OWASP MASTG identifies specific tool categories and example tools relevant to mobile SAST and DAST. Tool outputs should be reviewed by qualified personnel; automated findings should not be accepted or dismissed without human review.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-08

Products shall undergo code review conducted by suitably qualified reviewers who are independent of the code's authors; the review scope shall encompass at least misuse patterns and all critical findings shall be remediated prior to release.

Source: REQ-KEV-010 (40000-10)

## Guidance

Conduct the review using qualified personnel independent from the authors (who may belong to the same organization). The review scope may include constant-time evaluation, and unit/integration test coverage.

Define and document the qualifications, independence criteria, and review scope requirements for personnel conducting code reviews. Qualification criteria should specify: relevant security-focused training or certification (e.g., familiarity with CERT Secure Coding Standards for the applicable language - SEI CERT C, CERT C++, or CERT Java/Android as applicable), demonstrated experience with mobile platform security models, and familiarity with the vulnerability classes relevant to the product's technology stack. Independence criteria should specify that the reviewer was not the primary author of the code under review; reviewers from the same organization are permissible provided the independence criterion is met. Review scope documentation should confirm that the review addressed: adherence to secure coding standards, misuse patterns relevant to the product's threat model, constant-time implementation of security-sensitive operations (e.g., cryptographic comparisons, PIN verification), and the adequacy of unit and integration test coverage for security-relevant code paths. Records should be retained as evidence of V&V activities.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-09

The V&V process shall document and identify all test methods and selected test tools for cybersecurity V&V activities, including the rationale for their selection relative to the product's risk profile and design, and any deviations from the planned test scope together with their justification.

## Source:

- CLA-05-RQ-06 (40000-1-2)
- SOTA

## Guidance

A test strategy document can be used to record the selected methods (e.g., tools, techniques such as fuzzing, penetration testing, static analysis) alongside the rationale for their selection relative to the product's risk profile and design. This documentation supports traceability, internal and external review, and continuous improvement of V&V activities.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-10

Cybersecurity V&V activities shall recur throughout the product lifecycle in alignment with the vulnerability management activities described in 6.9 and shall not be limited to final development stages.

For this purpose, a documented schedule for recurring cybersecurity V&V activities shall be established that specifies, at minimum, the trigger conditions for re-testing (e.g., new release, significant code change, newly disclosed vulnerability affecting a component, change in threat landscape) and the V&V activities required for each trigger type.

## Source:

- CLA-05-RQ-04 (40000-1-2)
- SOTA

## Guidance

V&V activities should be planned to recur throughout the product lifecycle - not only at final development stages - including after maintenance activities, resolution of newly uncovered vulnerabilities, or substantial product modifications.

Trigger conditions should be defined in a V&V policy or test strategy document and should include: (a) each planned product release; (b) any change to security-relevant components, including third-party libraries or RDPS components; (c) disclosure of a CVE or equivalent vulnerability affecting a component integrated into the product; and (d) a defined maximum interval (e.g., annually) even in the absence of other triggers. For mobile applications, the organization should additionally consider platform-level changes (e.g., new iOS or Android major version releases) as a trigger for re-assessment of platform-dependent security controls.

The OWASP MASTG recommends continuous or release-gated security testing as part of a mobile DevSecOps pipeline.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.7-CR-11

A security test and review plan shall be developed that is grounded in the product's context, its cybersecurity architecture and design, the defined cybersecurity requirements for the product, the results of the risk assessment, and the results of tests and reviews. The plan shall define what tests and reviews are to be performed, what methodologies to apply, how often, and at what intervals, calibrated to the risk profile associated with the product's intended use.

## Source:

- PRE-9-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)
- PRE-9-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)
- PRE-9-RQ-04 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The plan may cover a class of products or an entire portfolio where that scope is appropriate. How frequently tests and reviews are conducted should reflect where the product is in its lifecycle, any shifts in the risk environment or threat landscape, and lessons drawn from security incidents.

The inputs to security testing are dynamic and may change over time. Test cases and methodologies should be reviewed and updated as technology advances and as the understanding of relevant vulnerabilities and threats develops, so that the plan continues to reflect the current security landscape.

### 5.8 Secure Production and Distribution {#s-5-8}

## Introduction

Secure production and distribution activities manage cybersecurity risks from the point of production through to market placement. For digitally distributed software, this means protecting the integrity and authenticity of software artefacts (including information and instructions) both in transit and at rest – protecting against manipulation by external actors.

A secure production control plan is a practical tool to support these activities. It typically captures cybersecurity-relevant production instructions, measures to prevent unauthorized alteration (addressing physical access, cryptography, and access controls), and methods to confirm the product is produced in accordance with its cybersecurity requirements.

Output: software distribution artefacts, documentation of measures used to protect the authenticity and integrity of the artefacts – in transit and at rest, plus documentation how information and instructions to the user are made accessible.

See OpenCRE 473-177 at opencre.org/cre/473-177 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-01

Software products and software updates that are distributed as software images or other distribution artefacts shall be protected against manipulation throughout the entire distribution lifecycle, covering both network transit and storage at rest. For this purpose, a documented build and release pipeline shall be maintained, including automated integrity controls and verification at defined points in the pipeline, including compilation, packaging, signing (conformant to 6.8-CR-05), and release or upload to the distribution channel.

## Source:

- CLA-06-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)
- PRE-10-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)
- RLS-1-RQ-04 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (requiring a documented standardized pipeline process)

## Guidance

Consider using integrity controls for distribution artefacts, such as cryptographic hashes or digital signatures, so that any unauthorized modification can be identified whether it happens in transit across a network or while the artefacts are stored or hosted. Assessing the cybersecurity of the digital distribution channel, for example an app store or a manufacturer’s download site, can support a determination of whether the hosting environment is appropriate and can reveal issues to be addressed through the product cybersecurity risk assessment.

Consider implementing a CI/CD pipeline (e.g. using GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Fastlane, or Bitrise) in which each stage produces a cryptographic hash (e.g. SHA-256) of the artefact and compares it against the hash of the input to that stage. The pipeline should fail and alert on any mismatch. Pipeline configuration files themselves should be version-controlled and protected against unauthorized modification.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-02

Where justified by the product's risk assessment and cybersecurity context, the production and distribution activities for digital software products shall incorporate access authentication.

Source: CLA-06-RQ-02 without the authenticity overlap already covered in CLA-06-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Which measures are suitable should be decided based on the product’s cybersecurity risk assessment. Multi-factor authentication is also a typical control used to limit access to protected areas of a hosting platform. If the risk assessment indicates that the risk is lower, it may be adequate to implement only some of these measures.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-03

Where applicable, user-facing information and instructions distributed digitally shall be protected against manipulation or unauthorized disclosure during distribution, including protection of the communication channels through which they are delivered.

Source: CLA-06-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Digitally distributed user documentation-such as manuals, safety information, and configuration instructions-should be treated as part of production and distribution processes. Organizations should consider protecting this material with the same authenticity and integrity safeguards applied to software artefacts and should ensure that the delivery path used to provide it (for example, a manufacturer website or an in-product update channel) is evaluated for cybersecurity risk.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-04

Where applicable, information and instructions intended for the user shall be delivered and presented in a manner that is accessible to the intended user population.

Source: CLA-06-RQ-04 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Accessibility covers both:

- technical access - the distribution channel should remain available to users and should not be limited in a way that blocks them from receiving the information; and
- usability - the information should be presented in a format and language suitable for the intended audience.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-05

A code-signing process shall be established and maintained for mobile application distribution artefacts that defines:

- the lifecycle management of signing credentials, including Android signing keys/keystores and iOS distribution certificates and provisioning profiles, as applicable;
- the roles authorized to approve and perform signing operations; and
- the conditions under which signing is permitted.

Signing keys used for Android (keystore) or iOS (provisioning profiles and certificates) shall be stored in a secrets management system (e.g. HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) and not in the repository.

Source: SOTA

## Guidance

The signing process should specify approved key generation parameters in accordance with the ENISA “Agreed Cryptographic Mechanism” guidance, storage requirements (e.g. HSM or equivalent managed key service), rotation schedules, expiry monitoring, backup and recovery arrangements where permitted, and revocation procedures.

For Android, the organization should consider enrolling in Google Play App Signing so that Google manages the app signing key while the organization retains control of the upload key.

For iOS, the organization should document the management of Apple Developer Program accounts, certificate and profile expiry monitoring, and the process for renewal or revocation.

Production signing and release should be subject to multi-person approval, and access to signing credentials should be restricted to authorized personnel and systems.

Mobile application signing keys, including Android app signing keys/keystores and iOS distribution certificates and provisioning profiles, are high-value cryptographic assets. If compromised, an attacker may be able to distribute malicious applications that appear to originate from the organization, subject to platform-specific controls. These assets should be protected using HSMs, secure enclaves, or other hardware-backed key management systems where feasible, with strict access control, auditing, and separation of duties. organization

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-06

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) and role-based access controls shall be enforced for all accounts with the ability to publish, update, or manage mobile application releases on distribution platforms (e.g. Google Play Console, Apple App Store Connect), and an access review process shall be maintained for these accounts.

## Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Access reviews should be conducted at least annually or upon personnel changes. Accounts should follow the principle of least privilege; for example, testers may require access to internal testing tracks but should not have production release rights. Service accounts used by automated pipelines should use short-lived credentials or API keys with restricted scopes rather than full administrative access. Orphaned accounts (e.g. for former employees or contractors) should be revoked promptly. Audit logs from the distribution platform should be retained and reviewed periodically for anomalous activity.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-07

The product shall be made identifiable by recording, at minimum, the manufacturer's name, the product name, and a version for recognizability and traceability to support for example vulnerability handling, down-stream software bill of materials (SBOM) generation and verification, and vulnerability information sharing and reporting.

Source: PRE-6-RQ-01 (40000-1-3) – with version made mandatory

## Guidance

The mandatory identification fields listed in the requirement can be supplemented with additional identifiers. Appropriate identifiers include release version, build number, Software Hash Identifier (SWHID), and release date. One or more of these may be used as needed.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-08

A communication mechanism shall be provided through which security-related information - including advisories, release notes, installation guidance, and notifications - is made available for the product.

Source: PRE-10-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Appropriate mechanisms for distributing security information may include a dedicated product security page, mailing lists, RSS feeds, or a vendor portal. Through whichever channel is chosen, advisories, release notes, installation guidance, and security notifications should be made accessible to affected users in a timely manner.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.8-CR-09

Where the product type, connectivity, and operational context make it feasible, a mechanism enabling security updates to be distributed automatically or semi-automatically shall be provided.

Source: PRE-10-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Where the product's architecture and its intended deployment environment permit, an automatic or semi-automatic update mechanism should be considered. Such a mechanism would allow security updates to be delivered to, or retrieved by, the product without the need for manual action. Whether this is applicable will be determined by factors including product type, network connectivity, and the operational context in which the product is used.

### 5.9 Product Cybersecurity Monitoring and Issue Management {#s-5-9}

## Introduction

Cybersecurity issues encompass vulnerabilities and incidents affecting a product and its related dependent products and services (RDPS) throughout the product lifecycle. Monitoring the threat landscape is essential to detect new vulnerabilities and respond to changes before they result in incidents. This monitoring typically involves identifying, receiving, and processing cybersecurity-related information from both internal and external sources - including vulnerability databases, lifecycle status of third-party components, end-of-support notices, cybersecurity laboratories, and market surveillance authorities - whether through manual or automated means. Issue management complements monitoring by ensuring that identified issues are handled and resolved, forming a key pillar of ongoing product maintenance.

Output: documentation of the activities undertaken including time aspects, and results of any assessments.

See OpenCRE 888-770 at opencre.org/cre/888-770 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.9-CR-01

Periodic procedures, automated where possible, shall be performed for monitoring of internal and external information that may affect the product's risk assessment as defined in 5.4 to 5.7, covering at least cybersecurity incidents and vulnerabilities, at intervals that are justifiable given the product context. Documentation shall include activities, frequency, sources, and the roles responsible for execution and review.

## Source:

- CLA-08-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)
- RCP-2-RQ-01 (40000-1-3) (internal and external, where possible automate)
- RCP-3-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (Documented procedure and automated where possible)

## Guidance

Monitoring can involve reviewing vulnerability databases, notices that integrated components have reached end of support, and other sources of vulnerability reporting. Relevant information may also be obtained from cybersecurity laboratories, comparable products available on the market, and market surveillance authorities.

Automation is important for minimizing the likelihood of missed vulnerabilities and to ensure timely identification of new threats.

The sources may include NVD, vendor advisories, OS platform security bulletins for iOS and Android, OWASP dependency vulnerability feeds, Google Android Security Bulletins, Apple Platform Security updates, and advisories from cross-platform framework vendors (e.g., React Native, Flutter). Automated tooling (e.g., software composition analysis tools integrated into CI/CD pipelines) may be used to supplement manual monitoring. The procedure should be reviewed annually, or more frequent, or upon significant changes to the product's technology stack.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.9-CR-02

The risks of verified cybersecurity incidents, changes in the threat landscape, and discovered vulnerabilities shall be assessed aligned with the risk assessment methodology established under 5.4 to 5.7.

## Source:

- CLA-08-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)
- CLA-08-RQ-03 (40000-1-2)
- SOTA (guidance on automation)

## Guidance

Aligning the assessment with the risk assessment approach employed during product development ensures that the severity and impact of newly identified issues are evaluated consistently within the product’s established risk context.

Where possible analysis steps should be automated as much as possible, to allow for timely action. Ideally, procedures are established that use defined exceptions where manual steps are required.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.9-CR-03

Upon discovery of a new vulnerability, documentation of that vulnerability shall be produced and communicated to relevant parties where the risk assessment and cybersecurity context make such communication appropriate.

Source: CLA-08-RQ-04 (40000-1-2)

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.9-CR-04

Verified cybersecurity incidents and discovered vulnerabilities shall be treated in a timely manner, with the urgency and nature of treatment proportionate to the risk assessment outcome and the specific cybersecurity context of the product.

Source: CLA-08-RQ-05 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Treatment decisions should align with the results of the risk assessment. The required response, including how quickly action is needed and what form it should take, may differ according to the seriousness of the vulnerability or incident and the product’s particular cybersecurity context. As reflected in relevant standards, regular testing and review can help enable timely treatment.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.9-CR-05

Where cybersecurity incident or vulnerability have residual risk, that risk shall be communicated to stakeholders using the communication processes and channels established under Clause 5.9, where relevant.

Source: CLA-08-RQ-06 (40000-1-2)

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.9-CR-06

At a minimum, the following designated internal and external sources shall be drawn upon when monitoring for vulnerabilities: the EU Vulnerability Database, externally reported vulnerabilities, outputs from regular testing, and regular review activities.

Source: RCP-2-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The items listed here should be treated as the minimum starting point. Organizations are encouraged to draw on other information sources where these are relevant to the systems they use or the threats they face, for example supplier-issued security notices or threat intelligence tailored to their sector.

### 5.10 Secure Decommissioning {#s-5-10}

## Introduction

Secure decommissioning planning ensures that when a product - including its Remote Data Processing Solutions (RDPS) - changes ownership or reaches end of life, user assets are not compromised. This encompasses the secure deletion of user data, settings, and cryptographic keys, as well as restoring the product to a secure default state.

When a product and its associated RDPS reach the end of their support period, manufacturers may have obligations to inform users about this transition and its implications for continued use. Such communications need to be clear, simple, and accessible. Planning for decommissioning therefore extends beyond the product's active life, covering manufacturer responsibilities at and after end-of-support.

It is worth noting that an RDPS may be integrated into multiple products; decommissioning focuses on appropriate removal of user data in context. Additionally, only authorized users - as determined by product context - may perform decommissioning or factory reset operations.

Output: documented communication method of decommissioning, documented rationale, documented activities for decommissioning permissions, user instructions for decommissioning – if any.

See OpenCRE 424-242 at opencre.org/cre/424-242 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.10-CR-01

Secure decommissioning shall be prepared by identifying cybersecurity aspects of decommissioning, all confidential assets requiring deletion and their location, establishing appropriate actions for any third-party-operated components, defining the method of user communication and what that communication needs to include, and documenting all manufacturer-side activities required to achieve secure decommissioning.

Source: CLA-09-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

When planning for secure decommissioning, manufacturers should identify the logical locations of all confidential assets within the product and any related RDPS, including user data, configuration settings, and cryptographic keys. Because an RDPS may support more than one product, the decommissioning process should address removal of user data only where that is appropriate in the context of the product. In some cases, decommissioning the product should include deletion of user data stored on the RDPS; in others, it should not. In all cases, it is considered best practice to tell users how to remove their data securely.

If third parties operate any part of the product, suitable contractual or technical measures should be in place so that those elements can also be securely decommissioned.

The method used to notify users about decommissioning - for example, through the product, by email, or in documentation - should be appropriate to the product context and intended users. Where a product is approaching the end of its support period, it is considered best practice to explain, in clear, simple, and accessible language, the consequences of continuing to use it.

Decommissioning, or restoring the product to a secure default state, should be performed only by authorized users. Which users are authorized depends on the product context, and not all users will necessarily have that authority.

Manufacturers should have a process that ensures the information for the prepared decommissioning is kept up to date.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.10-CR-02

Where user-facing decommissioning instructions are required, those instructions shall address, as applicable: removal and export of user data, removal of security-relevant configuration data, disconnection from the operational environment, secure disposal of the product, and advance notice of any automated data deletion including its scope and timing.

Source: CLA-09-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

### 5.11 Third-Party Component Cybersecurity Management {#s-5-11}

## Introduction

Third-party components - whether commercial, free, or open-source - can introduce cybersecurity risks that compromise the integrity of a product. Managing these risks requires due diligence throughout the component lifecycle: from selection and integration through to end-of-life. Key considerations include evaluating a component's intended purpose, its compliance with legal and cybersecurity requirements, its support status, and the maturity of its vulnerability handling practices. Manufacturers are advised to align responsibilities with their suppliers before bringing a product to market, and to account for the distinct nature of open-source components, where formal support arrangements may not be available but source code transparency offers alternative assessment opportunities. Information sharing about discovered vulnerabilities - including contributing fixes upstream - supports collective cybersecurity improvement and helps prevent fragmentation of the FOSS ecosystem.

Output: evidence that the relevant activities have been performed.

See OpenCRE 613-285 at opencre.org/cre/613-285 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-01

Before selecting and integrating any third-party component into a product, due diligence shall be carried out on a number of aspects when applicable. This shall include verifying alignment of the component's intended purpose with its planned use in the product, confirming the absence of known vulnerabilities, and determining whether additional cybersecurity testing is needed. For commercial components, the availability of CE marking and an EU Declaration of Conformity shall be checked. For FOSS components, assessment shall be performed of maintenance activity, availability of a vulnerability disclosure process, stewardship by a recognized organization, evidence of cybersecurity-by-design practices, and availability of security updates. In addition, license obligations shall be identified, documented, and managed prior to integration and throughout the component lifecycle.

## Source:

- CLA-10-RQ-01 (40000-1-2)
- SOTA (licenses)

## Guidance

To confirm that no known vulnerabilities are present, it may be appropriate to consult public vulnerability databases, including the European vulnerability database created under Article 12(2) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555. Further cybersecurity testing can also involve methods such as binary analysis, source code scanning, rebuilding from source, and code review. In choosing components, take account of the length of their support lifecycle so that risks linked to deprecated components or outdated technologies can be foreseen.

License evaluation should be performed as part of the due diligence process and should cover both direct and transitive dependencies. The procedure should identify license types (e.g., GPL, LGPL, MIT, Apache 2.0) and assess compatibility with the product's distribution model (e.g., proprietary app distributed via app stores). For FOSS components, the procedure should assess whether copyleft obligations could affect the mobile application's source code distribution requirements. SPDX license identifiers may be used to standardize license recording in the SBOM.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-02

Both the third-party component itself and the manner in which it is integrated into the product shall be addressed within the risk assessment and risk treatment activities required by Clause 5.

Source: CLA-10-RQ-02 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

The risk assessment should consider how the third-party component is incorporated and used within the product, rather than evaluating the component solely on its own.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-03

Third-party components and their integration into the product shall be included in verification and validation specified in clause 6.7.

Source: CLA-10-RQ-04 (40000-1-2)

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-04

Ongoing monitoring of third-party components shall be maintained for the duration of the product's lifecycle, so that vulnerabilities relevant to the product can be identified, in line with the monitoring activities set out in clause 6.9. This is a continuous obligation and does not end once initial integration is complete.

Source: CLA-10-RQ-05 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Monitoring is to continue throughout the entire product lifecycle, rather than being limited to the initial integration stage.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-05

Where a vulnerability is discovered in a commercial third-party component, the vulnerability shall be documented, disclosed to the responsible third-party, and remediated following the applicable vulnerability disclosure and handling procedures. The responsible third-party may be a supplier, service provider, or any party capable of facilitating handling of the vulnerability.

Source: CLA-10-RQ-06 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Newly identified vulnerabilities should be reported to the appropriate third party responsible for addressing them. This could include a supplier, a service provider, or another party able to support the vulnerability handling process. Relevant parties may put information-sharing arrangements in place through formal agreements, such as a coordinated vulnerability handling process. Section

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-06

Where the manufacturer discovers a vulnerability in a FOSS component and develops a fix, that fix shall be communicated to the open-source project concerned. Where it is possible to do so, the fix shall also be contributed upstream to the original project, under the terms of the applicable source code license.

Source: CLA-10-RQ-07 (40000-1-2)

## Guidance

Contributing fixes back to the original open-source project can be used as a legitimate way to address risk, especially in later versions of the product. Providing the fixes that were developed, or documentation describing those fixes, promotes transparency, contributes to broader cybersecurity improvement, and reduces the risk of fragmentation across the FOSS ecosystem.

## Requirement CR-ID: 6.11-CR-07

Third-party component suppliers shall be assessed for maintenance activity (level of support or having reached end-of-support) on an annual basis.

A documented policy shall be established and maintained to define the maximum permissible period between the public disclosure of a vulnerability in a third-party component and the release of a remediated version or the implementation of an accepted compensating control, differentiated by vulnerability severity.

If a supplier fails to meet the timeframe or support is below the documented threshold, a risk assessment shall be performed on the potential consequences of this support issue, which may lead to eventually deprecating the corresponding component(s).

## Source:

- RCP-2-RQ-04 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (assess supportability and timeframes)

## Guidance

Where open-source components lack a declared end-of-support date, organizations should assess ongoing maintenance activity as a practical substitute. Indicators such as latest release version, recent commits, responsiveness to reported issues, and active community participation can serve as evidence that a project remains supported.

Remediation timeframes may be aligned with recognized frameworks such as CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue examples or the organization's own risk acceptance criteria. Example differentiation: critical vulnerabilities (CVSS ≥ 9.0) within 14 days; high vulnerabilities (CVSS 7.0–8.9) within 30 days; medium vulnerabilities within 90 days. For mobile applications, the policy should account for the additional lead time required for app store review processes (e.g., Apple App Store, Google Play Store) when calculating remediation windows. Where a patch is not yet available, the policy should require documented risk acceptance or the application of compensating controls (e.g., feature flag disablement, server-side mitigation). NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF) RV.2.2 reference remediation timeframe policies.

## 6 Vulnerability Handling {#s-6}

### 6.1 Operational Security of Vulnerability Handling {#s-6-1}

## Introduction

Information in vulnerability handling is inherently sensitive, as it can be exploited by malicious actors. Both internal processes and external communications therefore need to incorporate operational security measures throughout the vulnerability handling lifecycle. These controls may be lifted once remediation and advisory information have been made public.

Output: documented operational security measures.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.1-CR-01

Operational security measures shall be maintained across all activities involving the receipt and communication of vulnerability information or reports.

## Source:

- PRE-3-RC-01 (40000-1-3)
- PRE-5-RC-01(CVD) (40000-1-3)
- PRE-5-RC-02(CVD) (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Implementing operational security controls should not harm accessibility. Organizations should keep submission mechanisms open and usable, and where appropriate, provide the option for anonymous reporting.

Appropriate technical controls for achieving confidentiality and integrity include HTTPSprotected web forms and encrypted or digitally signed email using S/MIME or OpenPGP. Further implementation guidance can be found in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, section 5.8.

Where sensitive material is involved - such as exploit code, credentials, or configuration data - the organization should transition the exchange to a secure channel regardless of the medium through which first contact was made.

Further guidance is available in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, section 6.7.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.1-CR-02

Access to vulnerability information shall be restricted, when it has not yet been publicly disclosed, where applicable, to only those individuals who require it in order to fulfil their responsibilities within the vulnerability handling process.

Source: PRE-3-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)- but access restriction made mandatory instead of considered

## Guidance

Non-public vulnerability information should be made available only to those with a demonstrated need to access it as part of their role in handling the vulnerability. Applying this principle reduces the likelihood of accidental or premature disclosure. Further guidance is provided in EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020, section 7.3.

### 6.2 Facilities for Vulnerability Handling {#s-6-2}

## Introduction

A vulnerability handling policy is an internal framework that establishes how an organization identifies, assesses, investigates, and remediates security vulnerabilities in its products or systems. It helps ensure that vulnerabilities are managed in a consistent, timely, and coordinated way across teams. A clear policy supports effective security practices, improves response to newly discovered issues, and helps maintain alignment between internal processes and external vulnerability disclosure efforts.

Output: documented vulnerability handling policy and its implementation in the form of facilities.

See OpenCRE 732-148 at opencre.org/cre/732-148 for related resources and topics for guidance.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.2-CR-01

A vulnerability handling policy shall be established, implemented, and followed.

Source: PRE-1-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

To help the vulnerability handling process operate effectively, consider establishing an organizational framework that gives clear ownership and accountability for the related activities.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.2-CR-02

The vulnerability handling policy shall describe the organization’s overall direction, principles, and responsibilities for handling potential vulnerabilities in products; set out how information about those vulnerabilities will be safeguarded against disclosure before remediation is available; establish a planned timeframe for remediation development; and explain the approach to the regular testing and review activities defined in 6.7.

Source: PRE-1-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

When applying this requirement, the policy should be made more robust by addressing the following:

- Describe the end-to-end process in a way that is consistent with broader vulnerability management expectations and clearly assign responsibilities for managing suspected vulnerabilities.
- Ensure that safeguards against early disclosure are consistent with the coordinated disclosure requirements.
- In setting a target remediation timeline, take into account the embargo period, including how it may be affected by coordination complexity with upstream stakeholders, the vulnerability's severity, and the characteristics of the product. This timeline is intended to guide remediation development and should reflect factors such as implementation difficulty and evaluated risk.
- Where feasible and suitable, identify downstream stakeholders that use the in-scope product. Whether this is suitable may depend on privacy or confidentiality obligations.
- Provide a mapping of upstream stakeholders to support the component identification activities.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.2-CR-03

Continuous monitoring shall be in place whether the vulnerability handling process is operating effectively.

Source: PRE-1-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Consider establishing concrete, measurable indicators or metrics that enable evaluation whether the vulnerability handling process is achieving its intended outcomes. EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020, clause 7.2 offers further direction on how to approach effectiveness monitoring.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.2-CR-04

The vulnerability handling policy shall support all activities defined in the vulnerability disclosure policy described in 7.3

Source: PRE-1-RQ-05 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

During the drafting or periodic review of the vulnerability handling policy, confirm that every activity prescribed by the coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy (5.3.3) is either directly addressed or actively supported by the internal policy. Maintaining this alignment ensures that internal operational processes and external disclosure commitments are coherent and reinforce one another.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.2-CR-05

A documented process shall be established for evaluating, approving, and recording decisions to delay full vulnerability publication under the conditions specified in 7.7-CR-05, including defined criteria for the risk evaluation, designated approval authority, maximum permissible delay duration, and a procedure for communicating the disclosure date to affected users of the mobile application.

Source: SOTA

## Guidance

Having this process for this decision, adds the procedural controls necessary to exercise the permission in a trusted, consistent, and auditable manner – even under high time pressure when the necessary decision expertise may not be available.

The evaluation defined in the process should be conducted by a cross-functional group including security, legal, and product management representatives. For mobile applications, the process should account for the time required for app store review and deployment when determining whether a delay is justified and when setting the public disclosure date. The record of the evaluation and approval decision should be retained as evidence. EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, Clause 7.5, provides guidance on timing of disclosure and conditions under which delay may be appropriate.

### 6.3 Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Facilities {#s-6-3}

## Introduction

Coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) involves a policy that communicates a manufacturer's intentions, responsibilities, and expectations around vulnerability disclosure. It covers both two-party coordination (between reporter and manufacturer) and multi-party scenarios involving multiple stakeholders. The policy is published externally, while supporting internal processes are established to effectively coordinate disclosure activities.

A key principle underpinning CVD is the use of an embargo period: reporters notify manufacturers privately and withhold public disclosure until a fix is available. The stages of receipt, verification, and remediation development take place within this embargo, ensuring vulnerabilities are handled securely and responsibly by all parties involved.

Output: documented CVD policy and its implementation in the form of facilities.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-01

A coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy shall be established, implemented, followed, and made publicly available in an accessible form

Source: PRE-2-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

When making the CVD policy publicly available, accessibility standards should be taken into account to ensure the policy can be reached and used by the widest possible audience. EN 301 549 v3.2.1 provides applicable requirements and advice on accessibility.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-02

The CVD policy shall include contact mechanisms accessible through multiple sensory modalities, ensuring users with diverse impairments are not excluded.

Source: PRE-2-RC-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Supporting more than one sensory channel ensures that individuals with particular impairments are not prevented from using the available contact mechanisms. As an illustration, a person with a writing impediment who cannot use a web form or e-mail could instead use a telephone number to both request and supply information. EN 301 549 v3.2.1 provides relevant accessibility requirements and advice.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-03

The CVD policy shall explicitly set out what parties can expect with respect to ongoing communication throughout the vulnerability disclosure process.

Source: PRE-2-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The detail underpinning what ongoing communication expectations should cover is addressed within the vulnerability handling process context. Section 7.5 provides further elaboration on the specific communication expectations that should be reflected in the policy.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-04

The CVD policy shall address each of the following areas: the expected contents of a vulnerability report; options for secure communication; the scope of the program; publication arrangements; and recognition of reporters.

Source: PRE-2-RC-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The purpose of a vulnerability report is to help understand, judge, replicate and solve the issue. Typical contents are contact information, product identification, description, replication procedure, any artefacts such as screenshots, description of the effect and how serious it is.

Further elaboration on the recommended elements to include in a vulnerability disclosure policy can be found in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, clause 9.3.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-05

A disclosure process shall be established so that details about a vulnerability are not made public until the vulnerability has been remediated.

Source: PRE-2-RC-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Disclosure strategies should be applied with flexibility, as no single approach is universally appropriate. The content of reports, agreed timelines, and the nature of responses can all be adapted to the specifics of each case, with agreement reached among all parties involved. Embargo durations are not fixed and may be negotiated individually between the manufacturer and the reporter, or through a coordinator where one is engaged.

Additional guidance on embargo periods is available in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, clause 5.6.8, and on disclosure strategy in ISO/IEC TR 5895:2022, clause 7.3.2.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-06

Secure communication mechanisms for vulnerability disclosure shall be made known to reporters and stakeholders.

Source: PRE-5-RQ-01-RE (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Reporters and stakeholders should be actively informed of the secure communication channels available to them. Although the provision of such channels is mandatory, their adoption by the reporter cannot be compelled. Secure communication should be maintained throughout the entire vulnerability handling lifecycle, not merely at the point of initial receipt.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-07

The vulnerability reporting process shall include an option that allows reporters to submit information without disclosing their identity.

Source: PRE-5-RC-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Providing an anonymous submission route - for example, an unauthenticated web form - reduces the threshold for reporters who may be hesitant to identify themselves. This increases the likelihood that vulnerabilities are reported and thereby strengthens the overall effectiveness of the disclosure program.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-08

Security controls applied to communication channels shall not create unreasonable barriers that prevent external parties from contacting the organization.

Source: PRE-5-RC-04 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The selection of secure communication mechanisms should balance security objectives against usability for external stakeholders. Controls that are disproportionately restrictive risk discouraging legitimate reporters, thereby undermining the purpose of the vulnerability disclosure program.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-09

A public reporting channel shall be made available, using the accessible methods specified in 7.3-CR-02, so that vulnerability information or reports can be received.

## Source:

- RCP-1-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)
- PRE-2-RQ-02(at least one) (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Different reporting channel types should be considered to maximize accessibility and reach. These may include web forms, issue tracking systems, dedicated vulnerability reporting services, role-based or alias email addresses, and telephone or equivalent contact options. Including a security.txt file per RFC 9116:2022 can make the reporting mechanism easier to discover. When designing these channels, accessibility standards as set out in EN 301 549 v3.2.1 should be observed.

Further guidance on policy elements can be found in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, clause 9.2.2.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-10

A system for assigning and maintaining identifiers or tracking numbers to reported vulnerabilities shall be implemented to support ongoing traceability of each report.

Source: RCP-1-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Assigning a unique identifier, label, or tracking reference to each report ensures that it can be consistently traced and referenced throughout all stakeholder communications during vulnerability handling and disclosure. Additional implementation guidance is available in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, clause 6.2.4.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-11

Receipt shall be confirmed of a potential vulnerability report to the reporter within a response window that is defined and published as part of the coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy.

Source: RCP-1-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Guidance on how to acknowledge receipt of vulnerability reports is available in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, clause 6.2.5.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.3-CR-12

Vulnerability reports submitted through channels that do not meet the security standards described in 7.1 should still be accepted rather than rejected on the basis of the submission method alone.

Source: RCP-1-RC-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The purpose of this requirement is to ensure that potential vulnerabilities are not missed due to procedural issues with how they are reported. An imperfect intake channel should not outweigh the need to identify, assess, and remediate security risk. Treat the report as valid input, then move subsequent handling into the appropriate secure process.

### 6.4 Intake in Vulnerability Handling {#s-6-4}

## Introduction

The intake of vulnerability reports focuses on evaluation for validity, reproducibility, and applicability. The manufacturer reviews the credibility of the report, attempts to reproduce the issue, and assesses both the impact on the affected product and the severity of the vulnerability. Only positively verified vulnerabilities proceed to the security risk assessment.

Output: vulnerability handling intake processes.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.4-CR-01

Where a vulnerability report does not contain enough detail to support assessment, the necessary additional information shall be requested from the reporter.

Source: VRF-1-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

If a report does not provide enough detail to carry out a meaningful evaluation, the manufacturer should take the initiative to contact the reporter and request what is missing. This could encompass technical reproduction steps, information about the environment in which the issue was observed, or clarification regarding the described impact.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.4-CR-02

A structured triage of each reported vulnerability shall be performed.

Source: VRF-1-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The triage should include the following elements:

- Credibility evaluation: Assess whether the reported vulnerability is plausible given the product's architecture, design, and known components.
- Reproducibility: Attempt to reproduce the reported issue using available product information, including the software list and product context.
- Impact analysis: Evaluate the potential impact of the vulnerability on the affected product, taking into account the product's security architecture and existing risk assessment.
- Severity determination: Assign a severity rating to the vulnerability to support prioritization in subsequent steps.

Where a vulnerability is determined to be not applicable, the rationale for this determination should be documented.

In multi-party coordinated vulnerability disclosure scenarios, additional guidance from ISO/IEC TR 5895:2022 should be considered.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.4-CR-03

Risk resulting from the vulnerability shall be evaluated aligned with the methodology specified in 5.4 to 5.7.

## Source:

- VRF-2-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (guidance)

## Guidance

Risk evaluation should be conducted in line with the existing approach so that the outcome remains coherent with the product's broader risk management framework.

For mobile applications, risk evaluation should take into account mobile-context factors (e.g., local vs. remote exploitability, dependency on user interaction, access to sensitive on-device data).

Standard scoring systems such as CVSS v3.1 or v4.0 provide a baseline but may not fully reflect mobile-specific exploitation conditions (e.g., a vulnerability exploitable only via a malicious app on the same device may score differently in a mobile context than in a server context). The OWASP Mobile Top 10(2016/2024) and OWASP MASVS risk model provide supplementary frameworks for contextualizing severity in mobile environments. The procedure should document how environmental and temporal CVSS metrics are adjusted for the mobile deployment context.

Assesment should take into account chained exploitation of the vulnerability with other vulnerabilities and not just the risk profile of the vulnerability on its own.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.4-CR-04

Each vulnerability shall be assigned a handling priority, derived from both the risk evaluation result and the risk profile specific to the product.

Source: VRF-2-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020, clause 7.1.4 e) may be consulted for supplementary guidance on how to approach prioritization decisions.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.4-CR-05

If the assessed risk level of a vulnerability surpasses the manufacturer's defined risk threshold, the vulnerability resolution process shall be expedited.

Source: VRF-2-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Expediting resolution means bringing forward one or more handling activities - including remediation development, testing, or deployment - ahead of the standard update schedule. The risk threshold that triggers this accelerated handling is determined by the manufacturer's own risk assessment framework.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.4-CR-06

When a vulnerability has been reported through a coordinated disclosure process, the originating reporter shall be notified of the outcome of the intake activity, if possible.

Source: VRF-2-RQ-04 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

In a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process, the reporter is an active participant in handling the issue responsibly. Informing the reporter of the verification results helps keep the process collaborative, transparent, and effective.

EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020, clause 7.1.4 f) provides supplementary guidance on how to communicate with reporters. In cases where the vulnerability concerns a third-party component, consideration should be given to also notifying the manufacturer or maintainer of that component regarding the verification findings relevant to their component.

### 6.5 Communication with Stakeholders in Vulnerability Handling {#s-6-5}

## Introduction

On-going communication is a continuous activity throughout the vulnerability handling process, running in parallel with all phases rather than following a strict sequence. Its purpose is to maintain regular communication channels with all relevant stakeholders - including users, reporters, coordinators, manufacturers, open-source stewards, and maintainers - as appropriate to the product's life cycle and the current phase of vulnerability handling.

Output: Vulnerability handling stakeholder communication processes.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.5-CR-01

Communication with reporters and all relevant stakeholders shall be initiated and sustained throughout the vulnerability handling process.

## Source:

- PRE-4-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)
- RCP-5-RC-01 (40000-1-3) – on coordinator communication

## Guidance

Communication channels should be opened at the earliest opportunity and remain active for the duration of vulnerability handling activities. Depending on the context, relevant parties may include vulnerability reporters, coordinating bodies, other manufacturers, open-source stewards, and maintainers of non-commercial open-source projects. The appropriate frequency and form of communication will depend on which phase of the vulnerability handling process is underway. Further practical guidance on structuring and sustaining stakeholder communication can be found in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, clause 6.5.

Where circumstances warrant it, an appropriate coordinator should be designated and actively engaged throughout the vulnerability handling process.

Coordinator involvement supports transparent and timely communication during vulnerability handling. A coordinator is particularly valuable when vulnerabilities affect multiple stakeholders or when direct communication between stakeholders is complex or otherwise not feasible. While engagement of a coordinator is optional, it can significantly ease the coordination burden in complex disclosure scenarios.

A coordinator should be considered when a vulnerability impacts several manufacturers at once, or when direct dialogue between the reporting party and the affected organization is impractical or overly complex. A coordinator provides a structured and impartial channel for communication and assists in managing the timing of disclosure. For further practical guidance on coordinator involvement, consult EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, sections 5.5.5 and 6.6. The coordinator role is formally defined in EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, Clause 8.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.5-CR-02

When communicating with users, communication channels and formats shall be employed that are accessible to a broad range of users.

Source: PRE-4-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Accessibility in communication requires that both the channels selected and the formats used are suited to a wide range of user needs and capabilities. Care should be taken to ensure that information relating to vulnerabilities is conveyed in a manner that users can meaningfully receive and comprehend. Additional guidance on how to achieve accessible communication methods is available in 5.9.

### 6.6 Remediation in Vulnerability Handling {#s-6-6}

## Introduction

The remediation decision phase encompasses the activities required to determine how identified and verified vulnerabilities will be addressed. This involves evaluating potential risk remediation measures, assessing their feasibility, and weighing their impact on the product, its users, and other stakeholders. This can result in a product update, a temporary mitigating measure, or a documented and justified choice to postpone or forgo remediation entirely.

Output: Vulnerability handling remediation processes.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.6-CR-01

A formal remediation decision shall be made and documented for each identified vulnerability, determining the course of action to address it.

## Source:

- RMD-1-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

- SOTA (documented)

## Guidance

In reaching a remediation decision, assess the available options in terms of their practicality and the effects they may have on the product, its users, and relevant stakeholders. Possible outcomes include releasing a product update, applying an interim mitigation, or making a documented and justified choice to postpone or forgo remediation. Further guidance on how to structure this decision process is available in EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020, clause 7.1.5 a).

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.6-CR-02

Following the remediation decision, a concrete action plan shall be established that specifies what steps will be taken and sets a defined timeline for their completion.

## Source:

- RMD-1-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (Guidance)

## Guidance

After a remediation decision has been reached, it should be converted into a practical plan of action. The plan should clearly specify the steps to be carried out and set a realistic schedule for completing them, taking into account the characteristics and severity of the vulnerability as well as the selected remediation approach.
