The remediation schedule should also consider the time lag introduced by app store review processes (Apple App Store, Google Play) before a remediation reaches end users; and whether OS-vendor-provided mitigations (e.g., Android security patch levels, iOS rapid security responses) reduce the urgency or alter the preferred remediation approach. These factors should be explicitly documented in the remediation decision record.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.6-CR-03

Once a decision to remediate a vulnerability has been made, the necessary activities shall be carried out to produce that remediation.

Source: RMD-2-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

- The manufacturer's established internal development processes should govern how remediation is carried out.
- Remediation is not limited to software patches or code fixes. Artefacts such as updated user documentation, configuration guidance, or changes to other materials required to adequately address the vulnerability should be considered.
- Where a supplier, open-source project, or other third party has already produced a suitable remediation, the manufacturer may adopt that existing remediation in place of developing one independently.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.6-CR-04

Where it is technically feasible to do so, security updates shall be delivered independently of functional updates, rather than bundled together.

Source: RMD-2-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Outputs may take various forms, including software updates, configuration changes, or documentation updates. Third parties, such as suppliers or open-source projects, may be involved in coordinating or sourcing remediation.

- When determining whether separate delivery of security updates is technically feasible, the assessment should take into account the available technology and relevant constraints, including cost, schedule, and performance limitations.
- The assessment may also encompass operational feasibility, considering whether a separately delivered security update can be successfully integrated into the product, sustained over time, and supported in the operational environment.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.6-CR-05

Any remediation applied to address a vulnerability shall undergo testing to confirm that the associated risk has been adequately reduced and that no unacceptable adverse effects on the product or its users have been introduced.

Source: RMD-3-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

Remediation testing ensures that a fix for a vulnerability is both effective and safe - confirming that the associated risk is adequately mitigated while not introducing adverse effects on the product or its users.

Where a fix is supplied by a third party, such as a component vendor, the manufacturer is expected to validate the remediation at the product level and confirm that normal functional behaviour is maintained, to the degree that this is reasonably achievable. Verification of the underlying component itself remains the obligation of the supplying party.

### 6.7 Release of Security Updates and Information in Vulnerability Handling {#s-6-7}

## Introduction

Security update release covers the collection of necessary artefacts to address vulnerabilities and their dissemination to users. Timely distribution is critical, as delays give attackers opportunity to exploit known weaknesses. Depending on the product type, its intended purpose, and its reasonably foreseeable use, updates may be applied automatically or manually. Where possible, security updates should be scoped to avoid changing other product functionality, minimizing unintended operational impacts - though some remediations inevitably require more substantial changes.

Output: Vulnerability handling security updates and information processes.

## Requirements

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.7-CR-01

Security updates shall be made available at no cost, except where a manufacturer and a business user have explicitly agreed otherwise for a purpose-built product with digital elements.

Source: RLS-1-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.7-CR-02

After a security update has been made ready, it shall be released to users without undue delay.

Source: RLS-1-RQ-02 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

- Updates should be handled according to the priority established in 7.4.
- Acting without undue delay means that vulnerabilities carrying the potential for broad societal harm are treated as high priority. Updates addressing critical security weaknesses should be expedited accordingly.
- Both automatic and manual distribution mechanisms are valid approaches. The appropriate choice depends on the nature of the product, its intended use, and the users it serves. Where a product supports automatic updates, that capability should be used.
- Commonly adopted industry benchmarks at the time of writing include: Critical (CVSS ≥ 9.0) - patch within 24–72 hours; High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) - patch within 7–30 days; Medium and below - patch within 90 days. For mobile applications, the procedure should account for app store review latency (typically 1–3 days for iOS App Store; shorter for Google Play) and should include a process for using expedited review requests where available.
- Server-side RDPS mitigations may be deployable independently of app store timelines and should be considered as a first-response option.
- NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 provides relevant patch management guidance.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.7-CR-03

Where the delivery of a security update is not entirely automated, clear installation instructions shall be supplied to users.

Source: RLS-1-RQ-03 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

When updates cannot be applied automatically, users should be given sufficient guidance to carry out installation correctly. Well-prepared instructions reduce the likelihood of errors that could disrupt the user's operational environment.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.7-CR-04

After a vulnerability has been resolved, information shall be provisioned in line with the coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy established under 7.3; where suitable, such information may be presented in summarized or aggregated form, in a format readable by humans, in a widely recognized machine-readable format, and include, as a minimum, the following elements to allow recipients to assess relevance and take appropriate remediation action:

- a description of the vulnerability
- a vulnerability identifier
- information sufficient to identify the affected product
- the potential impact of the vulnerability
- the severity of the vulnerability
- detailed remediation instructions
- the date of release and any subsequent update date

## Source:

- 40000-1-3: RLS-2-RQ-01, RLS-2-RQ-02(minimum), RLS-2-RQ-03 (human), RLS-2RQ-03-RE (machine-readable), RLS-2-RC-01 (EUVD)
- SOTA (mobile app guidance)

## Guidance

Clear and comprehensive publications - such as advisories or release notes - help users and stakeholders understand the nature of vulnerabilities and make informed decisions about managing associated risks. Coordination with relevant stakeholders and adherence to a coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy are central to this process.

Organizations publishing vulnerability advisories are encouraged to consult EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, Clause 7, for structured guidance on how to format and communicate disclosures in a clear and consistent manner.

Organizations seeking further detail on what to include in a vulnerability advisory should refer to EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020, section 7.4, which provides practical elaboration on the content and structure of advisory elements.

The required machine-readable format is defined in ISO/IEC 20153:2025. Organizations should consult this standard to ensure that published vulnerability information conforms to the specified format.

For mobile applications, residual risk notifications to end users may be delivered through inapp notifications, app store release notes, or security advisories published on the manufacturer's website. Notifications to enterprise operators deploying the application under mobile device management (MDM) should be coordinated through established B2B communication channels. Where regulatory notification obligations apply (e.g., under the EU Cyber Resilience Act or national cybersecurity authorities), the procedure should define the responsible role and the applicable notification timeline. The content of residual risk notifications should be proportionate to the audience's technical capability and should avoid disclosing exploitation details prematurely.

Published vulnerability information should be made available through the EU Vulnerability Database (EUVD).

Where vulnerability information has been disclosed via the CVE program, it will be ingested automatically into the EUVD. In such cases, no additional submission to the EUVD is required to satisfy this requirement.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.7-CR-05

Complete publication of vulnerability information shall be deferred in order to allow adequate time for security update distribution, in case all three of the following conditions are simultaneously satisfied:

- the risks associated with full disclosure outweigh its security benefits at that time.
- Sufficient information about the resolved vulnerability is made available to users in a manner that does not enable an attacker to exploit it.
- Users are notified of the scheduled date on which all vulnerability information will be publicly disclosed.

## Source:

- RLS-2-PM-01 (40000-1-3)
- SOTA (from optional to mandatory)

## Guidance

Where an organization invokes this permission to defer full publication, it should record and retain the justification for doing so. Such documentation is likely to be required as evidence when this permission is exercised, as indicated by the assessment criteria associated with this section.

For mobile applications distributed via app stores, the process should account for app store review timelines when planning coordinated public disclosure.

## Requirement CR-ID: 7.7-CR-06

Following the release of a remediation, post-release activities shall be executed that encompass maintaining the vulnerability case record and tracking the effectiveness of the applied remediation.

Source: PRA-1-RQ-01 (40000-1-3)

## Guidance

The post-release phase encompasses activities that take place after a vulnerability has been remediated and released. This phase is concerned with monitoring the effectiveness of released security updates, capturing lessons learned from the process, and using these insights to continuously improve future development practices.

The monitoring of a remediation does not need to be conducted as a separate, standalone activity; it may be embedded within the organization's wider vulnerability management process. Practitioners seeking further elaboration on post-release practices should consult EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020, section 7.1.7, which provides additional normative context for this phase.
